reviewText:
this is a great lens when used with manual focus. the auto-focus is consistently off at wide apertures. i had to send the lens to be evaluated by canon and its performance has improved since (canon acknowledged that my brand-new lens was not up to their own specs and had to be fixed). but still, three out of five shots are slightly off focus at apertures 1.4-3. there is no consistency in bad shots so it cannot be calibrated.

i get best results when i use a live view function and set the focus manually zooming on the spot. however, this is only possible when there is enough time, preferably a tripod, and this is kind of counter-intuitive given that one of the reasons to buy this lens is that it is so fast.

for people who are not sure if they want to spend all that money, i would recommend to get a much cheaper 1.8 50mm lens. its auto-focus works perfectly, at least for the one i had bought before wasting money on the 1.4mm lens. i compared the two lenses and the cheaper one outperforms at 1.8mm in terms of how crisp the images are. chromatic aberration looks about the same at 1.8mm. i don't care about the charts, this is what i see in the photos. the blurred background looks better with the more expensive lens but you should ask yourself if it is worth some extra $350!
summary: good lens but with some problems

reviewText:
one of the rules of photography is that for any serious work, you're going to be on a tripod.  tripods aren't possible in a lot of situations either by needing to be mobile or being in a busy environment and not wanting to be a trip hazard.  a monopod gives you most of the stability of a tripod when you can't use one.  try using one in a darkened aquarium.

i did my first wedding shoot using only non-is lenses with this monopod and had very few tossers due to blur.  yet i was still mobile enough to shoot a wedding.  i know how steady my hands are, and a similar keeper ratio simply would not have been possible without it.

it's also solid enough to use as a walking cane or possibly for self-defense.  it collapses short enough to not be a burden to haul around in my equipment bag, meaning that it goes where my camera goes.  absolutely worth the money.

update (december 30th, 2009):
the ball head slips on me.  it's decent but definitely not solid and i'd certainly be leery at putting a heavy lens on this.

it has also gone up in price from $30 to about $42 and is no longer such a great value.  you'll be better served spending the extra couple of dollars and going with something like a manfrotto setup.

reviewText:
i had read all the reviews, most notably the negative ones before buying this player.  the two main problems everyone seemed to echo were that the volume level was not sufficiently high and that the reception of the fm radio was not upto par.  there is some truth to both these points.
i don't like my music to be very loud, but once in a while when i am about to pass out at the gym, listening to say, "where the streets have no name" (u2) at an ungodly volume level typically energizes me enough to complete my workout.  notwithstanding that point, the volume level is quite satisfactory in my opinion.
as far as the radio is concerned, i needed a tuner as the tv audio at the gym is broadcast over a radio frequency.  there are some stations that sound great, some that have distortion, and some that it just doesn't receive.  but, the few stations that i like (probably the most popular ones and therefore the most powerful ones too) sound just fine.  i had problems with my sony arm-band walkman with the others too.  so, i guess it is not entirely the player's fault.  the tuner worked perfectly outside the gym. i think it is fine, but i wish it were just a little more powerful.
with the exception of the above nit-picks, this is a great player.  software installation and use is ridiculously simple.  the belt clip works great and so does the remote.  i am not an audiophile, so the headphones sound fine to me.  i don't use them however, as i have a better pair.  using the remote while running/stair-climbing/weight-lifting was easy.
all in all, a good little gadget.  if the two negative points above are very important to you (they are to me), you won't be completely satisfied.  but, you will still be happy.  i am.

all in all, a good little gadget.  if the two negative points above are very important to you (they are to me), you won't be completely satisfied.  but, you will still be happy.  i am. good value for the money

reviewText:
i am a amateur enthusiast in photography and have owned 3 dslrs prior to purchasing this camera. my main motivation was to get high quality images with a mirror less camera that was with less weight and size as compared to a dslr. i read many strongly positive reviews about the x100s so i purchased it, read the manual cover to cover, and took it with me on a week's vacation to colorado to try it out.

what i found was that it was a joy to take pictures with. i loved the manual controls where i could easily set aperture and/or shutter speed. the combination optical viewfinder with a digital info overlay was great. when i came home i thought i had found the ideal camera ... until i downloaded the images into lightroom.

several issues came up. first, about a dozen of the 300 or so pictures i took had corrupt image files. the images were tiled with different areas of the image being sliced up from other areas ... almost like a puzzle. several files lightroom flagged as corrupt or damaged image files. some wouldn't even open at all. this has never happened to me before with any prior digital camera and i know it was not my memory card or computer as both worked fine using other cameras.

the second issue was the camera's exposure. it consistently did a poor job of evaluative metering such that over half of my landscape images had no detail in the shadows. i had to use shadow recovery in lightroom on a majority of the images to try to correct the exposure to produce a usable image. i am aware that there is a dynamic range feature with the camera that allows for one to utilize multiple automatic exposures to produce a higher dynamic range ... but i didn't now set this up as default in situations that did not look to me like it would be needed. using the feature trades off shooting with at least 800 iso and flattens contrast. so perhaps if one was willing to trade off using two extra stops of higher iso and a lowered contrast ... then maybe this would produce better pictures.

the third issue is that whenever the camera overexposed the sky... sometimes it would keep the blue color true. sometimes it would shift the color of the sky to an cyan bias, which looked unreal.

the fourth issue is that the focusing mechanism was sometimes hit or miss. most of the time it worked great. i always just keep the center focus point activated and use the technique of focus and recompose. so my focus intentions are clear.  most of the time the camera focused very accurately and fast. sometimes it indicated it has locked focus ... but i didn't discover until i had downloaded the images that it simply missed and the subject i focused on was blurred.

the fifth issue is that i don't think it's quality is up to par with my dslr camera. i thought the glowing reviews of the new sensor and the prime lens would produce images that would rival my dslr. they don't. it does produce images that a slightly better, sometimes, than i can acquire with my iphone or my compact canon point & shoot $300 camera .... but i expected for $1,300 i would have image quality at or near my dslr.

so, i really wanted to like this camera. i think i could compensate for some of the issues if i used dynamic range ... took multiple shots of important images so i could not miss a good focus lock ..l. shot in raw so i could recover shadow detail and perhaps prevent color shift with highlight areas ... etc.  i could also realize that i need multiple shots because the camera sometimes produces corrupt images. but this is not right for a camera that is $1,300 .... $1,400 with a decent case. so it is returned to amazon.

i feel my review is fair for the camera that i had. i only hope that my particular camera was a lemon that had some issues in manufacturing that wasn't representative of most x100s cameras. if i only found one or two issues, then i would probably have had it replaced. however  since i had multiple issues it gave me the impression that perhaps this camera was really over-hyped in reviews cause it is light ... it is fun to operate  .. and it does look like a leica .... but in the end what mattered to me most was image quality. in that regard, this camera failed.

reviewText:
learned the hard way that even when "modular" psu manufacturers keep their cabling brand and sometimes even model specific. i have an awesome enermax revo modular psu but couldn't find indy-sleeved cables on the website or from other manufacturers. since i was going to build another pc i saw no reason to pass on the deal i found on amazon. of course the cables won't work on my revo psu. be very careful that if buying these cables it will work with specific corsair-only psus.

it is very difficult to figure out even on corsair's website which psus are compatible. i bought a low end corsair cx600m modular psu to be used as an emergency back up and was happy to find these cables fit. i probably got lucky. however the cables do appear to be of extremely good quality and i will be using them on my next build... i hope.

there really should be an industry standard of modular psu cables. this current practice serves no good service to anyone... except psu manufacturers. since i have yet to use these cables in an actual build i am only giving 3 stars. that could change in the future.
summary: still up in the air on this one

we had a newly purchased hp 15.6 inch laptop, so when i had the opportunity to acquire this item, it felt like the stars had aligned!  and when it arrived, it looked great. sleek and shiny.

so with much anticipation, the application of the sleeve began.  it did not work.  simple as that.  the 15.6" laptop would no longer close quite all the way, and frankly, we had to stretch the material so tight to just get it on, we were worried about damaging the computer.  to give the benefit of the doubt, i should mention that our laptop has a somewhat large bezel (the edge around the screen).  not all 15.6" are quite the same.  perhaps with a slightly smaller bezel, it would have worked.  but it says 15.6" and we have a 15.6", so i'm not willing to cut much slack.

and on top of everything else, it smelled bad!  i think  that was actually the final straw that had us take the darn thing off.  it didn't fit right and it stunk.  why keep it??!!

i'm not going all the way down to 1 star, because i can still see someone with a slightly smaller computer getting this to work, and if they had a not-so-keen sense of smell, they wouldn't mind.  so it was a complete bomb for us...but maybe not for everyone.

reviewText:
i have not tested the data capabilities for this product, so i have no information there.

this was purchased as a charging cable only, for travel purposes.  if you travel a lot (or even a little), you are always looking for ways to cut weight and bulk.  the biggest culprits for both these days seems to be cables, electronics, and power supplies.  this does its basic job of cutting the weight, bulk, and mess.

why only three stars?  well...

1. there is a small plastic loop to attach a keychain.  i have a belkin miniusb to usb also, so i was going to clip them together.  the small plastic loop broke immediately, so i clipped it off.

2.  the recoil system tends to get stuck.  so far, i have been unable to "unstick" it, but i suspect that soon, this will simply break.

3.  i am using this to charge a samsung galaxy note iii.  the charging port on this product is perfect.  i never had a problem... up to now.  i don't know if it is a bit over-spec, but it is not a tight fit.  it has to be put into the port nicely and cannot be moved even by accident, or the connection will drop and you will not charge.  i thought it was charging a whole night, but woke up to an almost dead phone before a meeting.  not good.  thank goodness for the kmax-812 4400mah rechargeable backup external battery i purchased here!!!

in conclusion, i am very, very careful with my electronics and cables.  to a fault, really, as i know that a broken cable or device while on a trip can really be a huge hassle and distraction.  so, to have these problems within the first week of ownership is not good.

i do not expect this product to last.  i will buy a better one (belkin, maybe) and use this one as an emergency backup as it is just not reliable enough for day to day use.
summary: ok for emergencies, but that's it

summary: severely hobbled by ios (ipad users beware)

reviewText:
have discharged/recharged this battery several times to condition it and now have it in use: as with past purchases of this brand and type of battery, it is performing extremely well in my video camera for *very long* recordings.
************
warning (10aug2015)
*************
just received a shipment from kastar for two (2) *advertised-as* ***lenmar*** brand batteries.
what i received was two **kastar*** brand batteries ... not lenmar brand.
the capacity rating stamped on the kastar batteriesis 1900 mah (my lenmar dlf60 have a rating of 1100 mah).
the kastar battery is *noticeably* lighter in weight.
a li-ion battery that weights less will have 70% more capacity? we shall see..
have opened one package and will be testing: look for a further report.
**************
test results (13 august)
kastar-usa seller admitted that there were no lenmar batteries in stock. they sent kastar brand batteries instead. they claim the batteries are very good and invited me to try them. i took that as permission to try one of the two batteries without voiding the return policy.

i used two video cameras which i have employed over the past six years to make several thousand youtube videos. the cameras have always been powered by lenmar dlf-40 batteries. one camera is a creative vado hd generation 1 and the other is a generation 3. the cameras are substantially different: the gen1 camera draws a lot of current and the gen3 camera uses less power for the same length video recording.

in these tests one camera had a kastar battery and the other, a lenmar bettery. the cameras were side by side in the window looking out onto a highway so that the scene being recorded had motion to encode. the total length of recording was determined by when the battery was depleted enough that it refused to record and the camera turned itself off. each recording was about one hour which ran the cameras out of memory. i would delete the recording and immediately start recording again. repeated until finally the battery gave out.

three days of testing lead to this summary:
lenmar battery in gen1 camera: usually depleted at 2 hours, sometime a bit less.
kastar bettery in gen1 camera: usually depleted at 2 hours, sometime a bit more.

lenmar battery in gen3 camera: usually depleted at 2 hours, sometimes a few minutes more.
kastar bettery in gen3 camera: usually depleted at 3 hours, sometimes a few minutes more.

results:
under high discharge conditions, lenmar and kastar are equal.
under low discharge conditions, kastar  lasts noticeably longer.

the time to recharge the kastar battery was always at least 35% longer then lenmar.

decision:
the lenmar battery has a rated capacity of 1100 mah.
the kastar battery has a rated capacity of 1900 mah.
on average the kastar battery charge should last longer ... and take longer to charge.
it seems that the 1900 mah rating only applies if the camera does not have high current draw.

what important question is left unanswered? some li-ion batteries degrade  quickly over time with repeated (daily) heavy use. others can take the discharge-charge cycles longer before swelling and quitting. for that only time will tell.

i'm going to accept these unasked-for-substitution batteries because they seem adequate for now.
summary: as expected lenmar is quality **if the seller actually ships lenmar batteries**

pros:

-mycloud service along with its mobile apps takes all the hard work out of connecting to your camera away from home. you can always configure it to your liking if you mind the security issues of having the data routed through d-link's servers, but it's truly plug-and-play.
- slim, light weight form factor makes for easy mounting and positioning. the build quality is excellent.
- night vision with infrared led (similar to sony's nightshot in that it mechanically removes a filter) really does work well, though you would also be seeing only in monochrome.
- sound pick-up is pretty good. makes for usable sound detection.
- h.264 compression makes for smaller video files and lower data transmission rates.
- added function as a wifi-extender, which is essentially a repeater, useful in expanding your wireless network to cover dead spots at a sacrifice of speed.. if you manage to get hardwire ethernet at the site of the camera, you've effectively turned it into a full speed wifi access point, which is even better.
- wireless n means ease of positioning. reception has been decent.

cons:
- gets pretty hot, though it has not presented issues with crashes.
- the image quality really leaves a bit to be desired. granted it's not meant to be hd, nor does it have optical focus, but this is just a mid-low end webcam quality--from 5 years ago--with all that fuzziness, low color saturation, and sub-par low-light performance (without nightvision turned on). it's serviceable, but a low end pc webcam from a reputable brand should do at least as well and more likely better.
- mydlink app feels unfinished and can use not only more options but also more polish.

this is akin to a mini computer with webcam and network capability. therefore the software and firmware really makes a tremendous difference in its functionality. thankfully d-link has provided with my-dlink feature that makes for easy set-up--i was able to set up remote viewing with minutes. the software has the most basic features: activate motion or sound detection, activate night vision, and turning the sound on or off. the interface looks unfinished, however, and there are multiple versions of my-dlink app on the google play store, with some that's already obsolete (why is it still there to confuse people?). i hope d-link eventually polishes up the interface software and maybe add more features and controls. however as it stands, it does deliver on its promises--you can easily view from the web (via smartphone, tablet or pc) without any issues or the toil of setting up port forwarding. some image quality and software quibbles aside, the decent build quality, good wireless connectivity and repeater feature, as well as a solid night-vision ir mode--this is a truly functional camera without many useless frills. it can be better, but it's already pretty good.

as a mechanical keyboard, this thing is perfect. the red switches feel like the primo-mucho-expensive red switches, with perfect response time and no ghosting issues. they have a slight rubberized texture to them so they feel nice and the see-thru parts of the keys let the light shine through beautifully. the rgb coloration options are very basic, but can match with any setup. the brightness can be adjusted as well as the speed of certain effects (waves, breathing, etc). for the price i've paid (60ish bucks) it is fairly reasonable, especially since compact keyboards are often... weird. as far as wired mechanicals go, this little rectangle friend gets an easy 5 stars.

i've used many mechanical keyboards of all sizes but this one feels great and responds wonderfully. the usb it comes with has a firm shape to it and is wrapped up with nylon, so it's easy to manage and doesn't tangle easily. wanna know what's even better? the cable is just a standard no-tangle android charger/non-i-product charger. so if the cable gets messed up, you're not sol like you would be with other wired keyboards. a rat chewed through my 2nd mechanical keyboard's cable so i had to trash it, but this one i don't have to worry about that randomly happening ever again! great stuff.

1 minor downside is there's no multi-media keys which is crazy for 2017, or heck, even 2014. but thankfully auto hot key (every computer owner should have this!) can easily transform my page up/page down keys into volume keys - pretty much the only important multi media keys lol. i use:
pgup::volume_up
pgdn::volume_down
appskey::~

so volume keys, check. and my useless menu key can become a tilda or ~ character. yay! you can also turn "useless" keys into phrases. like my ins key will always type a cute  since there's no numb-pad for me to do it.

so why did i give my rectangle friend 3 stars?

well, it is advertised as a bluetooth device but its bluetooth usage is extremely limited. you're going to have an awkward time or maybe impossible time (like i did) for hooking it up to a computer. it's friendly with android devices version 5 and higher for me. so android? wonderful. computer? noooope.

then there's the firmware/software issue. no disc was provided and there's no firmware on the website. i had to do a little digging to get the software to work, and sadly, it was not 100% for my keyboard. it did work but left my \| key blinking random colors when i tried to reassign my page up/down keys. so either this is a very new product or a very old one.

if any of this changes i'll change my review. but for now this stays at a 3/5 overall.
summary: it's an amazing wired keyboard! however...

i probably should have known better, but i went ahead and bought this radio, having looked at the mixed reviews.
it's an interesting device, but the price is rather steep, but i was hoping that at least it would be of high quality.
wrongo
i dutifully fully charged it before doing anything, and that's when i ran into problems.
after familiarizing myself a bit with the functions, which seemed reasonably easy too go through and understand, i first copied files onto the internal storage, which seemed to go okay, albeit taking roughly twice as long as the same amount of data can be moved to my sub-$30 mp3 player, a bit of a disappointment given the huge price difference.
having done that, i inserted an sdhc card and tried copying the same files to it to test it out, and that's when it locked up.
i tried holding in on the play button to force it to shut off, but that didn't work, so i pushed in on the reset using a paperclip, which was very difficult, but it finally did reset it.
i tried to copy the files again, and it immediately locked up once more, necessitating yet another reset, at which point something must have come undone internally because it went blank and quit working entirely; and no amount of plugging it in to rejuvenate the charge or pressing of buttons would work, just flat out dead as the proverbial door nail.
disappointed, i went through the one process that was trouble-free, i.e. initiating a return request through amazon, which itself couldn't have been any easier.
i printed up the automatic return label, boxed everything up in the the box that the whole thing had originally come in, then let ups take it from there.
too bad that c. crane couldn't get it together with this overpriced paperweight, because i have a standard cc radio plus that works great, quite unlike this, and -- while expensive -- still doesn't cost quite as much as this clunker.

reviewText:
as a student, 802.11 ac router at this price sounded like a good deal to me. i have the router with hardware version 2. the range was good and speeds were impressive. the setup took less than a few minutes and i was connected within 10-15 minutes. the usb connection also works fine provided you have a hard disk with < 2 tb capacity.

the router was slightly glitchy at the beginning. it used to drop connections every once in a while and i had to turn off the router once a week. it wasn't a deal breaker, but still annoying. for about 4-5 months, it worked fine (provided i restarted it or gave it a night's rest once a week).

the problems arose with the recent firmware update (140929). as soon as i updated the firmware, all my devices started dropping the 2.4 ghz wireless network giving authentication errors. i read a bunch of forums and tried many things people suggested. but the problem was never fixed. so i contacted the customer support via email. i guess there was a time zone difference so the troubleshoot was going at the rate of one email per day. after numerous attempts changing the type of security, changing configuration, channel, channel width, enabling/disabling  wmm, short gi and a bunch of other settings (around a hundred permutation and combinations), i finally gave up. i reset the router to factory defaults and downgraded the firmware. now things are back to the usual restart once a week.

i recommend this router if you want a 802.11 ac router on the cheap. but it has its quirks.
summary: 11 ac router at this price sounded like a good deal to me

reviewText:
make sure you buy it with the knowledge that you won't be able to use it to the full extent a wide angle lens is used to. otherwise you will be severely disappointed with this lens. but just how so?

i know a photographer that uses this lens for wedding photography with her 10d. for her the lens does the job wonderfully. the lens takes sharp pictures, is light enough to haul around in a wedding, and wide enough on a 1.6 form factor camera to provide sufficient field of view for such event. the field of view on a 1.6 form factor camera would be equivalent to 45mm on full format; almost normal view.

i on the other hand used my 28mm lens for nature photography, and let me tell you the results were not just disappointing but down right useless! simply stated, you will not be able to use high contrast/saturation landscape and nature pictures that are procuded by this lens.  the bright sun will cause sever chromatic aberration in your pictures. hence, the fringes of trees and light poles for example will display the dreaded discoloration (with this lens the color is generally purple). every tree branch at the top corners will become purple at the fringes. those are truly unacceptable results.

now for the big question, is it possible that i had a bad copy? probably not. after being so disappointed i researched this lens extensively (especially on fred miranda site) and found that others had the same problem. in fact, its overall score on that site was 7.4 at the time of my research, thus my 3 star rating. after learning the facts i decided to return the lens instead of exchanging it with another one. since then i have ordered a 17-40 l.

should you order it? this lens is a great value. in fact, i rank it as a best value lens after the 50mm 1.8 in the lower end range of canon prime lenses. nonetheless, don't expect to take stunning nature photos with it; otherwise chromatic aberration will stun you!

ps. i agree with most of what a previous reviewer mentioned in his post, but wonder if he owns a good copy. this lens has been in production for a while and there may be a difference in quality between various batches out there.

reviewText:
this 15" notebook computer bag for the most part lives up to the typical case logic standards for quality materials and good construction but it surprisingly falls short on some crucial aspects of the design even thought the pockets and organization are well-thought out and the bag is lightweight.

note that the amazon illustration above shows the previous edition--the current model has a flap on the expansion slit side with corner buckles, only one small handle, and the shoulder strap attaches differently.

that shoulder strap would work well enough if it had a textured pad to keep it from slipping but the single, offset, flimsy hand grip is awkward and unusable except to briefly assist in holding the case while putting the shoulder strap over the arm.

the padding seems insufficient at the bottom and side edges of the case--in my experience, trauma to a closed notebook computer on the large area of the flat top or bottom does little real damage beyond a cracked shell if it doesn't take out the screen but trauma to an edge can easily destroy latches, switches, led displays, ports, drives, or hinges.  i suppose padding doesn't really help much if great force is involved, anyway.

the expansion zipper adds a good deal of weight, bulk and complexity while only adding a small amount of additional capacity and i think it is unnecessary given that current notebooks are slim.

the asymmetrical design of the stretch slits is very unattractive in such an otherwise sensible bag but they are half-covered by the flap.  i still would prefer to see something like the chevron pattern on the other side of the case.  that shocking fluorescent orange lining color has grown on me while the grey exterior is very much to my taste.
summary: good quality materials and construction but some design flaws.

reviewText: these are tiny speakers with one wide range 4.5 inch driver, and nothing's going to change that; if you don't like the typical bose sound (lacking low bass and crisp highs), you're not going to be happy with these. that said, they're ok sounding for what they are: they fit in tight spaces and they do get loud with a good amount of wattage behind them, and if you add a subwoofer, they're even better.  just don't ask that one little driver to do too much-the highs get shrill and the overall sound turns into a mush if turned up too high.  if i didn't have other speakers to compare these with i might be more impressed than i am, but other speakers really point out the limitations of these.  i notice the same limitations in the bigger 901's (which bose tried to overcome with their special equalizer) that i do here.  i would never spend more than $50 on these, and i'm not sure i would even go that high.
summary: don't ask too much of these speakers, and add a subwoofer for satisfactory listening.

i deem the hawking tech hwp54g card completely worthless: stay away from it.

take my advice and stay away from any product from that bogus company!

first let me say that my closet is filled with wireless equipment that just does not work.  i bought this unit thinking that motorola was a good company and i heard good things about their routers, and of course my bad luck with linksys, dlink, netgear.

reviewText:
i purchased this at best buy about 6 months ago and while the sound is really great (and i would say superior to the bose), the software/firmware of this device is absolutely horrendous.

so first off, don't waste your money on buying 2 of these and trying to link them up. it won't work. it will start to work, then just cut out after about 3-4 minutes and you have to re-pair the devices. i ended up giving one of my ue booms to a friend because it was past the 45 day return window at best buy.

second, the sound level on this thing is really weird. when it's connected to my iphone 6 plus or my samsung galaxy 6, the volume will just randomly shoot up to max volume and scare the ever loving s**t out of you. it's well documented on the ue/logitech forums and the standard answer from support is "just reboot the device and re-pair it with your phone." that's not a solution.

but when connected to a pc or mac via bluetooth, it seems to work flawlessly.

all that said, i used one of these at an outdoor camping event/party with over 100 people and this thing rocked. the sound was loud and it projected in all directions, so i can only imagine what the bigger version of this thing can do.

so while i'd love to give this thing 5 stars on the sound quality, i need to give it 1 star on the functionality since it doesn't pair up like they say it does and it randomly shoots the volume up to the max scaring small children and animals.
summary: sound quality is phenomenal but firmware/software/functionality is horrendous

reviewText:
if this continues to work as well as it has so far, we will be very pleased.  the only small glitch we had was setup.  following the instructions that come with it, we could pair both sets of headphones, but sound only came through one at a time.  by reading the reviews here, we were able to get everything working, but it did take a little while.  the review by g. hopkins-camandona gave us the info we needed to get both headphones working at once.  once you get them paired, you have to push the button on the transmitter twice in a row if you want them working simultaneously.  sometimes we lose connection on one of them, but i think the key is being sure that there is a clear path between the transmitter and the headphones.  as long as we are conscious of that, it doesn't seem to bother.  not sure how this would work for longer distances.  we're using it while sitting right at the computer.  for what we need, this works great, and you can't beat the price.

update:  still working great after two years

reviewText:
i read the other reviews and haven't experienced any of the same problems, but i'm running firmware 1.44 and haven't used the device more then a few hours.

i received the linkstation tonight and was eager to get it working. i usually don't read instructions, so i quickly hooked up the power, ethernet and a usb printer (rear port). plugged the ethernet cable into my linksys wireless router using the default straight through cable setting. i downloaded from [...] the latest manual and drivers. you really don't need any drivers or even the installation disk if you know how to check for a leased dhcp address from your dhcp server (in my case the linksys router). just simply type in a browser [...]  the user name is equal to root and password is blank.

next, i went in to configure the date and time, configure a new static ip address (i don't recommend ever using a dynamic ip on a network server). then change your administrative password. if you are going to user the product as a ftp server, enable this and set up some more shares. for security reasons i recommend disabbling anonymous log on. configure user authentication and user group permissions. i didn't try the support for pdc windows type authentication, but it looks easy to configure. if you are not going to use a windows domain, then make sure you configure your "workgroup" to match your home machines. the default on newer machines is mshome, but you can change it to anything as long as you are consistent.

the printer which i had seemed to configure itself. the most difficult part was installing the local print driver, which in windows xp professional was fairly simple. i pointed to the manufactures driver, which i downloaded from brother.

my only complaint is that the linkstation does not support dynamic dns. this would be a great feature for those of us that cannot afford a static ip address from our isp's.
summary: easy to configure, worked no problem

while i do agree that the hole is a little small but i would rather have that instead of too big. drilling in to plastic or fiberglass will most likely be a little bigger due to friction. a rat tail file for metal works very well, just check the fit often.

for a great solid centered cut, i predrilled a hole in the center where i wanted the camera & then used the hole saw. i've seen reviews that say the saw is junk, i guess it is if you are not using it correctly. i wasn't going thru anything thick at all but it was metal. i did not force it, the speed was medium & i stopped every once in a while to let the saw cool down. if you go too fast & the saw gets hot, that is when you'll most likely to have issues. also check to see that what you are inserting it in to is the thickness of the camera's feet. you will want to run a test or two to try & get the angle of the camera view on your monitor the best you can. afterwards if there is any play, you can use a grippe shelf liner (tool boxes, kitchen drawers) to adjust from outside as long as it is not too tight of a fit.

it works great on my honda cr-v but i had to mount it under the license plate on the hatch back & it is a little noticeable, i didn't want to go with it in the bumper because of the fear that someone would bump the car & break the camera.

for any reason i were to need a new camera or to replace one, i would highly put this on the top of my list & would buy this again!
summary: do not be in a rush / hurry.

i absolutely loved my canon angle finder and everything about it except for the adapter springs- they're made of soft mallable metal and they don't hold their tension.  they loosened up after only using a couple of times and i worried about dropping it, or worse, losing it.  i tried bending the springs back, but they quickly loosened again.  well, while touring my gardens and hiking through the woods last week, shooting small flora and fauna, mine fell off the camera somewhere along the way and is lost forever.  i should've known better after feeling the way i did about the springs.  i truly loved this piece of equipment and used it very often and i'm really upset that i have to buy another.  i'm very hesitant to do this and may indeed check out other options but i've always used all canon products so i'm in a quandry as to what to do.  if you buy this do not leave it on your camera under any circumstance- it should be removed and stored everytime you move your set up.  tsk tsk canon, your cheap springs cost you a five star rating and have upset a long time faithful customer.

oct 11, 2010 update: my wife found the angle finder in one of our gardens when doing a fall clean up!!!  it was covered in mud, was filled with moisture/water and had two baby slugs living in it (eww!).  initially it didn't look good but i decided to see if i could fix it and found a schematic online.  i took it apart, cleaned it all very carefully and thouroughly and let it dry out for a few days.  i just finished putting it all back together and it literally works as good as new.  talk about tough!  the weakest thing on this amazing accessory is the adapter springs but i'll give it an extra star now for toughness (4 stars).  so glad it's back and that it had been on backorder or i would now have two.  things sometimes work out.  ;)
summary: excellent with one major fault- weak adapter springs

reviewText:
not wanting to lug my slr around on a recent trip to disney i opted to pick a nikon p330 given the following features

larger than average sensor (bsi as well)
gps (i travel a lot and use maps to find photos fairly often)
fast lens (f1.8 at wide angle)

the p330 seemed to roll-up all of the features i wanted, but implementation was a mixed bag

pros:
good image quality for a point & shoot (including lower light situations w/o flash)
pretty good movie quality (most of the time)

cons:
unbelievably slow lock on and write times - this was seriously painful and a lot of wasted time was spent
poor gps - another reviewer has a similar comment, but the gps implementation in this camera is a joke.  i got it to work twice over the course of 10 days.  once out on my back deck when setting the camera up and one other time while roaming one of the theme parks.  all other times (shot about 1500 pics over 10 days) the gps had no signal - mind you this is outside with a full clear view of the sky.
movie artifacts - i noticed that the camera started to get pretty hot during some movie recording (~7 minutes long).  when i got home i noticed that several frames were corrupted towards the end of the recording.  video quality for the first ~5 minutes was excellent.

lastly while the camera appears solidly built i can only say that the camera met an early death when it took ~1 foot fall to pavement.

have moved on to a canon s100 - will give that a try (and pray that the lens error issue doesn't get me)

reviewText: okay, sure, this product currently offers free super-saver shipping. but please listen why it's worth going out of your way to get a far better-performing product, which is also far more environmentally friendly. if in the market for this battery, try to find a rayovac co101p2 battery pack. the rayovac's nickel metal hydride (nimh), so it's not toxic waste when spent. this one is toxic nickel cadmium (nicd). the rayovac has a (real) capacity of 1300 mah (milliamp hours), the highest i know of for this type battery pack. this generic one is rated at 650 mah (.65 amp-hours), and that will degrade quicker than nimh, and will have a shorter overall life. plus, the rayovac is around the same price, excluding the temptation for super saver shipping. i wish amazon sold the rayovac, but they currently don't, so one must look elsewhere--i found mine locally at fry's electronics, but they can be had online too. possibly becoming harder to find. please see my full review of the genuine (but toxic) panasonic replacement, vs the (superior) rayovac co101p2. some phone & recharging tips: - try to run down the battery as much as possible before recharging. this will keep the capacity high (true for both nicd and nimh). if you only ever talk for 20 minutes and then recharge it, at some point the battery will only last for 20 minutes (worse with ni-cads). full drains prevent this. - when the battery runs out of charge, or if it is very low, charge right away. it's better to store these batteries charged, than drained. - slower charging is easier on the battery, not that you have a choice. most phones charge very slowly. - when the charge is complete, remove the phone from its base/charger. the chargers are dumb, and continue charging, and overcharging will slowly damage the battery. if you go on vacation, take your phone off the charger (ideally after fully charging). - it can help to buy 2 phones of the same type and switch out handsets, or one phone with multiple handsets, to fully drain handset batteries. having a speakerphone built-into the base can sometimes help while swapping handsets. - almost all tools and personal hygeine devices with integrated or proprietary battery packs use toxic nicd batteries. it is illegal and unhealthy to throw those batteries away. someday soon, nicd batteries will not be made or sold in the us, voluntarily or not. they're already being banned in europe. good riddance anyway; they're barely cheaper, and inferior in every other way. - all rechargeable batteries (nicd or not) can and should be recycled. it's free, just drop them off at a real electronics store like radio shack or fry's electronics. - if you have a dead rechargeable device, and you can't get the battery out (like a shaver or electric toothbrush), you can usually just drop off the whole part. - even well cared-for batteries will eventually die, whether used or not. but how you treat them makes a huge difference. - other types of batteries are the opposite of nicd and nimh, in that it is best to drain them as little as possible, and recharge frequently. those include lithium-based batteries (cellphones and mp3 players) and lead-acid (car batteries). lead-acid batteries can be dropped off for free recycling at any auto parts store, and lithiums can be dropped off anywhere you could drop off nicd's.
summary: go with rayovac co101p2 battery pack (nimh) instead

reviewText:
i had a kensington turboring and loved it.  the turboball is their current warranty replacement as the turboring is no longer available.
using a trackball with the fingers is, for me, much more comfortable than using one operated with the thumb.  i get a pain similar to old atari joystick thumb cramps when using thumb-movement trackballs.  the finger movement on the turboball is quite smooth and very precise.
the scroll wheel on the turboball is in a useless location.  there's no way to use the wheel without moving the entire hand off the unit or contorting one's thumb into an extremely uncomfortable angle.  this makes the wheel all but unusable for any frequent use.
that and the roller mechanism used here is essentially the same thing as the turboring.  which means frequent cleaning and possible loss of the little red bearings.  the bearing races do appear more sturdy than those used on the turboring (which is what broke on mine).  but the rollers are still the same and probably just as likely to gum up.  mine tended to gum up once a week with daily (8+ hours) of use.
it's really a shame, the best feature of the turboring, and what sold me on it, was the scrollring.  kensington has seriously missed the mark with design of the turboball.  it'd have been ok if the scroll wheel wasn't in such a horrible location.
oh, but only if they'd put a scrollring around the ball of their expert series trackball!  i'd buy it in a heartbeat.  it too suffers from a poorly placed scroll wheel.
kensington warranty support is excellent but getting this as a replacement for my turboring just doesn't cut it.

i bought this camera as a replacement for my kodak playsport, which worked perfectly until i dropped it overboard. i was seriously disappointed with this camera, as the images were terrible. i tried it in all modes, hoping for an improvement, but the poor quality of the images was the only constant.  fujifilm says that the resolution is 16 megapixels, however the photos were fuzzier and grainier than the playsport's 2 megapixel photos. they all looked like they had been shot at a very high iso, even though i had set the iso to 200. edges of objects were jagged and filled with luma and chroma noise. black objects looked grey because of all the noise. whites were blown out. other colors were either faded due to the noise, or over saturated because they were over processed.

video quality was just as bad.  there were huge areas that were badly pixelated with no detail at all.  the video also skipped frames intermittently. looking at the video frame by frame, i found that it was not a playback issue - those frames were never recorded.

the optics weren't any better. the edges of the images were out of focus throughout the entire zoom range, making the photos look as if they were taken by a pinhole camera made from an oatmeal carton.

i returned this camera after two days of use.  i wish kodak still made the playsport.

the layout is also not the greatest.  i have a floppy/usb combo drive and the controller is too far for standard fdd cable when using the lian li pc-a05fna mid tower.

it's too early for me to completely give up but i expected better results. my last 5 builds were with asrock (lga 775) and asus (am3 and lga 775) and all went well.  i used the thermaltake meorb in all with excellent results.  the memory sticks were ddr2 for the asrock and ddr3 pc1600 (g skill ripjaws 4x4gb and corsair vengeance blue 4x4gb) for asus in comliance with manufacturer's recommendations. the asus also had the pc1600 listed as oc but had no trouble.

will contact tegra tech store for possible alternative if all else fails.

the design is nice and the bag can fit a lot of clothes. i got stuck with a united basic economy ticket (no carry-ons allowed!) through my employer and didn't have time to deal with checking a bag, but this just barely held enough clothes for a 5-day conference. the compartments are nicely designed and i like the look. for those reasons, i would have given it 5 stars, except that on my first trip with it the hand straps started to tear off! by the time i was on my return flight, one had torn all the way off. i was not abusing the bag at all, and the straps did not get caught on anything or something like that. they just tore over time under the weight of my clothes. why? because it seems they forgot to put any seam sealer, fold-over, or melt on the end of the nylon straps. so, being made of slippery fibers, they just pulled away from the stitches!

my verdict is only buy if you are savvy with sewing and repairing things like this, because you will need to. at the price, it's not worth dealing with returning it, i'll just try to fix it myself.

when my apple keyboard drowned in a few drips of coffee, i was on the lookout for a hardy replacement.  i settled on the icekey after reading many good reviews.  but for all its positive qualities, the one thing that drives me absolutely insane is when the keys stop working, and i have to unplug and plug it back in to the usb port.  i don't understand why this happens, because the mouse that is attached to the usb port on the keyboard does not stop working.  only the keys.  this sounds like a minor inconvenience, but i have to crawl under my desk, in pantyhose and a skirt, getting tangled in dusty computer cables, trying desperately in the darkness to find the correct cable to unplug/replug.  it is a major hassle.  plus, the cable that comes with the keyboard is way too long.  do they think i need to bring my keyboard with me into the next room?  i would rather have a shorter cord with optional extender.  also, the extra usb port on the keyboard does not work with my usb flash drive.  i never had that problem with my apple keyboard.

the keyboard has a great feel, but the bugginess is so irritating, i really wish i had just gotten another apple keyboard.

my network is a cat6 gigabit network, with 5 client pcs and 1 server hosting my media.  2 asrock 330hts are running openelec without breaking a sweat, my other 3 pcs are running xbmc via windows 8 without any problems.

sadly the kdlinks a100 cannot cut it.  i think i will try a zotac next.

reviewText:
update:

the player freezes with no sound and with the screen on (displaying album artwork), at random times and for no apparent reason. one of my two units had to be reset so many times that it can no longer be reset: it feels like that internal pad you press on with a sharp pin has now disappeared (it must have broken off). our only recourse now is to wait 3 days for the battery to run dead, and hope that it will be reset simply by recharging it from scratch. we've only had this unit since august (it's now december), so i no longer feel the reliability level of this product is sufficient to justify its purchase. buy something else that doesn't have to be reset all the time!

i bought the 2 gb model because the 4 gb version wasn't available yet and it had the largest flash memory of any unit that works with my napster-to-go subscription, so it can store the largest number of songs and color photographs.

why did i choose a flash memory based mp3 player? napster-to-go compatible hard drive models with much larger storage capacity abound, but i figure they'll break prematurely because they use a hard drive that can't withstand much jogging, accidental bumping or dropping.

i bought two of these players plus the separately sold ac wall charger, and attached one of them to the wall charger for 6 hours, while i attached the other one to a usb port on my pc to charge it for 6 hours.

at the end of 6 hours, the unit attached to the pc was fine until i unplugged it, then it went comatose and would not even revive when the reset button was pushed several times. i had to exchange it for a replacement unit just two days after buying it.

the unit attached to the wall charger was fine, and i went on to load it up with music using my napster-to-go subscription. that was fine until 2 weeks later, when my wife charged it on a pc using the usb cable. after charging and disconnecting from the pc, it too went comatose.

this time i was able to revive it by pushing the reset button.

then i took a look at the other unit, which had been charging on the ac wall charger. it had also gone comatose, and i was able to revive it by pushing its reset button.

the reset button is inside a tiny hole on the left edge of this unit. you can find it by following the thin groove that's below the screen all the way to the left edge of the unit, where you'll find it on the side. the picture in the manual does not accurately depict its location.

the hole leading to the reset button is very, very small. the instructions say to penetrate that hole with a pin.

i used the sharp end of a safety pin to do this. when the pin is inserted, it's quite easy to miss the reset button unless the pin is inserted at exactly the right angle. you'll know it's not at the right angle if you don't feel that you're pushing on a pad with a spring behind it when you reset the unit. that pad travels a short distance until it's stopped by a control surface inside the unit; that's when you know it has been reset.

the reset system should be redesigned so that it doesn't depend on the angle you insert the pin to work. i suspect that the first unit i returned could have been reset if i had known that you have to insert the pin at just the right angle to do it. since i didn't know, my several attempts to reset it were not successful.

resetting the unit is akin to rebooting a pc: it revives it when the internal software (called "firmware") has frozen by restarting the software. it does not erase your songs or photos.

make no mistake: this mp3 player looks, feels and works beautifully. however, since the firmware is newly designed, it appears to have bugs relating to disconnecting it from usb or charger power that cause it to freeze, and the reset button is a little hard to use if you don't know about the things i described above that could cause you to be unable to reset it. you may just end up with a unit that's frozen and not be able to reset it.

it needs to be a little more user friendly than that. hopefully a future firmware update will be available that will lower the occurrence of the unit locking up (freezing), especially when disconnecting from a usb port or ac charger after recharging it. as another user noted, the "safe disconnect" icon is often times not even in the system tray.

if you don't subscribe to napster-to-go, your options to get content for your mp3 player are to transfer your favorite songs from cds you own to your hard disk ("ripping the songs"), or purchase songs one track or album at a time, at a price ranging from 88 to 99 cents per song from napster, rhapsody or walmart.

you can also download books you want to listen to (such as best sellers and classics) or "podcasts" (your favorite newspapers read aloud, or your favorite radio programs like npr) from a plethora of sites (like netlibrary or audible) that make these available, onto your computer's hard drive. now you can listen to your music, audible books and podcasts over your pc loudspeakers while sitting at your pc.

then you can transfer your songs, audible books and podcasts from the hard drive of your pc to your mp3 player(s). this enables you to take your mp3 player with you to enjoy listening in your car, in your office, while jogging or working out at the gym, while shopping, or at the pool or the beach to hear your music, audible books and podcasts anywhere.

reviewText:
i have 7 wall mounted flat screen tv's in my home, and i've used several types of wall mounts, including articulating and flush mounts, to hang them, but this cheetah mount has been the most disappointing. it is made of thin metal that must be bolted together in the center to form the mount. the posts that bolt to the tv and hold it onto the mount are flimsy. if my 49 in. flat screen had been heavier (it's 36 lbs), i would have returned this mounts for something more substantial. i gave it 2 stars because i decided to use it, and my tv is still securely on the wall, but i would never purchase this particular mount again nor would i recommend it to anyone else.

update: march 31, 2015
soon after my review went live on amazon.com, a representative from spn performance, the amazon marketplace provider of cheetah mounts, contacted me via email and phone to discuss my review and provide some insight on why cheetah mounts are sold as bolt together units instead of the one-piece back plate mounts that they used to sell through amazon.  taylor, the spn performance representative, said the redesign of the back plate was mandated by amazon due to an effort to automate their storage, handling and shipping facilities.  smaller surface area on the back plate leads to smaller boxes, which is essential for automated handling of packages.
taylor explained the mount that i purchased has been through extensive testing, and would indeed hold 3 times the weight limit advertised in the product description.  taylor continued to work with me to find a cheetah mount that i could be happy with, and that's why i'm increasing my review to 4 stars.  good customer service seems to be non-existent these days, but taylor at spn performance went above and beyond.  spn didn't just provide good customer service, they provided great customer service.  how many times have you read or heard that lately.  my 49-inch tv is still securely hanging on the way, and i'm comforted by taylor's explanation of their testing, so give cheetah mounts a try.

i'm glad that amazon makes it so easy to return items with their print out labels and pre-paid postage.

now, i've just re-ordered the delphi xm2go version of the same unit from amazon(which was probably made by the same manufacturer)in hopes of better quality control.

oh btw - on a positive note, after the button dropped inside the unit, it did stop rattling. go figure.

reviewText:
i got this camera so that my kids can video chat with my parents who live in another state.  it was simple to install on windows xp and i haven't had any problems.  it works well with skype.  the video quality is decent.  the microphone is much clearer and louder than the one built into my laptop.  i'm sure there are better cameras out there, but i didn't want to spend too much money.  plus, video quality is usually limited by your internet connection, not the camera.  the only gripe, which some others have had, is that the button on top of the camera is easy to bump and it tries to load microsoft live messenger.  i changed it to open skype using another reviewer's suggestion:

jrverse says:
you can have the large button activate a different app (like skype) when it's clicked.

this works for me and others on the web (advanced users only!!!):
1. open regedit.
2. navigate to the following key:
[hkey_local_machine\system\controlset001\control\class\{6bdd1fc6-810f-11d0-bec7-08002be2092f}\????\settings]
where ???? is a number like 0000, 0001, 0002, 0003, 0004. you may have a few of these.
3. under each of the "\????\settings" folders, look for the entry called "quickstartpath", and change it from the current value (usually "c:\program files\microsoft lifecam\icepick.exe") to the path of the program you want to launch when the big button is clicked (like "c:\program files\skype\phone\skype.exe") this works perfectly for me.
summary: works great for skype video chatting

reviewText:
i'm using this with a several year old 42" vizio.

i give this 4 stars because:

a. it is very easy to assemble

b. the clasping mechanism for actually attaching the tv to the wall mount is well designed which allows for simple attachment, and detachment.

c. the tilt is a nice feature.  the tv is mounted in my bedroom and is high enough up the wall that the viewing angle from my bed would be compromised.  being able to tilt down takes care of that.  the tilt action is very smooth and sturdy.  i have absolutely no concern for my tv up there.

why it doesn't get 5 stars:

the center bracket that connects the two pieces has four holes drilled in it...two for each side.  it comes with nuts and bolts previously installed, all you have to do is tighten them down.  unfortunately, on one of those brackets the holes looked like they were drilled by hand and are too close to the corner so you can't get a socket over for tightening.  not a huge deal, but it's a quality control issue.  yes, i was able to tighten it down using pliers, but it added some installation time, and as i was in somewhat of a hurry that was annoying.

still, if i come across the need for another tv mount i'll probably go with a cheetah mount.  especially because it seems like a good quality product for a low price.

*****update july 17, 2015******
i am hugely impressed with cheetah's customer service.  i was just contacted by them as a result of my review that mentions a slight quality control issue regarding the location of screw holes.  they called (left a message) and emailed to inform me they were giving me a 50% refund for my "trouble."  considering the reviews number over 9,000 i can't believe they took the time to connect my review with my order number and then contact me aggressively with such a gracious offer.  as i mentioned in my original review i was already probably going to go with a cheetah mount in any future tv mounting needs, but after this i am absolutely going to buy cheetah.

well done.

reviewText:
i'm a reasonably tech-savy guy, but at home i like my life simple and my gadgets easy to use and the ipod mini is neither of these.  to be fair, i'm 47 years old and this was my big introduction into mp3 players, and maybe i'll stick to cd's like my father sticks to cassette tapes.  i also use a windows pc, which i understand doesn't work as well.  but with that said ...

right off the bat, the installation is a pain.  you have to install several different applications that require numerous pluggings and un-pluggings of the ipod.  at one point i was instructed to unplug the ipod from the usb port and plug it into the power adapter, something about a firmware reboot, but what the heck, it should be able to get power from the usb, right?  even the serial number is challenging for those of us over 40 ... you have to copy it from the back of the ipod and it's there in low contrast 0.2 point font.

i knew i was in trouble when i took the protective plastic sicky off the ipod and printed on it was a long list of reminders about special multi-button-hold-for-a-while commands to do obscure things like turn it on and turn it off.  basically the device has only one button and you just massage it in about 60 different ways to attempt to coax it into doing what you want it to do.

but it doesn't really care what you want to do.  after you finally get the software installed and the ipod plugged into your computer for the 13th time, it proceeds to take a tour around your hard drive, locate every obscure piece of junk song that happens to be there, and start downloading it to the ipod.  i had no idea that stuff was there, don't really know where it is, other than it's now on my new mini and i can't get it off.  i tried deleting the songs, but the mini woke up and downloaded it all again.

that's ok, when i tried downloading a cd that i owned, it took me 15 minutes to figure out that the file/import... command does something entirely different than the "import" button and the one that i wanted took forever to accomplish.  does anyone with a real job have time to download their music collection onto a computer?

it took me a while to figure out how to get that one button to adjust the volume, and then once i did i discovered that every time my finger came anywhere near the button the volume keeps changing.

so ... i think it's "cool", but i don't like it.  i'm going to download a couple songs that i'll use for jogging and such, but you have to really want to futz with it to take advantage of this thing.

the grado r1si has been a legendary headphone for many years. this new r1i improves on the sound of the old rs1 with more detail and better bass performance. i bought these after sort of lusting after them for many years. probably 15 years or so or whenever these were released. i already owned the newer ps-500, which are 5 star phones without question. the r1si arrived and my 1st thought was "wow, the packing box is nicer than the ps-500" - then when i opened the box the beauty of the headphones struck me instantly. they are absolutely gorgeous. and they are incredibly light. much lighter feeling in my hands and head than the ps500. i was thinking...man, even if these sound awful i will keep them for the looks as they look great with my ra1 amp.

yes, i own the ra1 amp paired with a dac feeding high res files from my mac. the amp is a perfect mate for my ps500 so i assumed it would be even better with the r1si.

my 1st listening test ... i was hugely disapointed. gone was the rich, liquid, sensual and full sound of my ps500. it was replaced with a sharp, dry, and hard to take midrange that was excessively forward. i let then burn in for a while..and each time i came back to them they sounded a teeny bit better but even still, they were no match sonically for the $100 less expensive ps-500. they look better, they feel better and  they come with the extra cables and better box but for sound, the ps500 rule the roost.

ps500 at $595 is a steal of a deal. they provide a rich, detailed but warm, thick and sexy sound while giving a nice wide soundstage (though not as wide as the ps1000 or hd800). the r1si's seem a bit closed in, lack the soundstage and are a bit sharp. female vocals turned up loud will pierce through your brain. rock is too bright. if i did not have the ps500s to compare i would not know any better and i would probably get used to the r1si sound and be happy but side by side it was no contest.

i appreciate the rs1i's for the look design and style (which i love) but you can do better for less. if you want them partly for the wood and look then they are worth it as they do sound good, just not as good as others.

pros:

light
gorgeous dark wood color
details are there
great for acoustic guitar
it's legendary :)
conversation starters
nice thick cable
easy to drive

cons:

fragile build
my copy had the drivers reversed so i had to disassemble to correct this. 2 minute job but where is the qc?
fatiguing sound, even with the matching ra1 amp and burn in (when compared to the $100 less ps-500)
$200 to expensive imo

if you like a sharp forward midrange sound these are for you. if you like a warmer but detailed rich sound with soundstage, the ps500's can not be beat for $595
summary: the ps-500 is leagues better for $100 less, i have both

reviewText:
with a long history of many failed attempts at ip wireless cams, linksys creates what others could not; one that works.

configuration with wep was pretty easy. it's a little temperamental with distance compared to the tolerances of other g devices, but it works. it does not react well to low light levels and tries to compensate via its own gain. if you are using this in a home without ample light, expect a grainy picture.

frame rate is about 20fps and is annoying. the security feature works. it senses movement and mails a captured video file. with only 4 seconds at the medium setting, the video images were over 500kb. this is not for a dial-up aol user.

there is a remote viewing option that lets you use their web servers to hit your cam from anywhere. of course expect to pay about $40 for two years access.
summary: it actually works and that's a surprise

reviewText:
i got the equiso smart streaming stick because i wanted to watch youtube, netflix, and other android functions on my tv.  however, this device does not always want to work, and even when it does, it doesn't perform that well.

1.  control issues.  using the remote to interact with the menus usually works, but sometimes there is a "sticky" effect to dragging items on the screen, that the menu continues to interact a full second after letting go of the center button.  gaming may also be difficult, as this remote wasn't really designed for it; it could likely do simple games, like angry birds, but not minecraft, or many of the other advanced games.

  also, some of the buttons do nothing, which is not convenient when watching videos (no forward/back buttons, have to use on screen controls).  keyboard setup is makes it so that you don't always know whether you're going to get a capital/lowercase letter, symbol, or number.  even worse is that sometimes that the alpha-numeric keys don't work, which makes it even harder to type in passwords.

2.  display issues. some times the stick does not display anything on the tv, and pressing the power button on the remote does nothing (same with holding the button down).  a lot of times, you have to unplug the thing from the tv before you'll get anything.  when it does work, it never goes into power saving mode, and never dims the screen.

  another issue was scaling the screen; it starts off displaying an image 40% larger than the screen, so you have to downscale it.  while adjusting it for the first time, it skipped on to the next part of the tutorial.  thankfully, i was able to go back by going into settings, and hdmi.  no setup up process should ever force you on to the next step, ever.

3.  video playback is not great.  even though the device supports 1080p, it will not play netflix at any quality higher than 480p.  youtube playback is erratic, and the device honestly acts as though i'm accessing the internet via mobile internet access, rather than broadband.  this means that high definition video playback will constantly stop to buffer.

does the device do anything right?  well, it does play videos, and run android applications, but this is when the device decides to work.  it isn't worth the price, and i'll be returning mine soon.

reviewText: after using this tripod to hold up my dslr camera (olympus e-500) for almost two years, i am finally ready to relegate it to the use for which it was designed, holding up my point'n'shoot camera (fujifilm e900). i knew when i made my selection that it was not enough tripod for my intended uses, but it was lightweight and it fit my budget, so i figured i could get along with it for a while. that while is over now, as i finally have another tripod for the dslr camera. (the new tripod is another manfrotto rig, a bogen-manfrotto 055mf3 3-section magfiber tripod without head paired with a bogen-manfrotto 488rc2 midi ball head with rc2 rapid connect system (3157n), coming in at almost 4x the price of the digi tripod and almost twice its weight.) the 718b tripod is a somewhat taller version of the bogen-manfrotto 728b digi compact tripod with integrated 3-way head and carrying bag (black), with a slightly different head configuration and a different quick release plate. i appreciate the extra inches of tallth. while nicely constructed, this tripod is lightweight and will not take the same abuse as sturdier models. the enamel on the cast metal parts chips easily (should have been powder coated), and my unit was damaged by a drop of about a foot (while in its storage bag!). the head is controlled by a single lever for both pan and tilt, with the pan loosening slightly before the tilt. the head motions are viscous damped to smooth out video pans. the center column and the legs are anodized aluminum, with triangular cross sections for added rigidity. the fourth sections of the legs look awfully skinny. i carry a hex key along to keep the leg pivots tight. one of the things i used the tripod for was taking panorama sequences, to be stitched together in photoshop. in order to stitch panoramic images easily, one of the requirements is that the camera remains level throughout the pan. after repeated attempts, i have concluded that this is largely impossible using this tripod. in gusty conditions, this tripod shakes the camera like a leaf. an aspen leaf. there is no hook on the bottom of the column to add stabilizing weights, which would have helped. for all of that, i am not ready to consign this tripod to craigslist. i am sure it will be quite satisfactory holding up my digicam, or the odd camcorder for shooting the odd birthday, etc.
summary: good enough for its intended use

i asked for this little seiki 20" tv for a christmas present after reading some so-so reviews here and wondering if i should get it... but i went ahead since it was very inexpensive. i opened it up at christmas, and it's packaged well - a very compact box that includes the remote and batteries with a manual and quick start guide.

i wanted this tv for a room where i have a computer and some ham radio equipment, so i wanted this tv to double as a monitor for that computer. after attaching the base (4 screws that are included to attach the vertical part to the base, then 3 screws to attach the entire base to the tv), i plugged it in and plugged an antenna into it (antenna is not included). for an inside antenna, i picked up a lot of channels, so the tv tuner is really pretty good at picking up signals that have decent strength.

for some reason i can't adjust the tint - the tint slider is greyed out - but right out of the box the picture looks pretty decent and doesn't need tint adjustment. i did have to back off the color a few notches, but i'm pleased with the picture on this seiki!

next i got a computer monitor cable (also not included) and connected the vga connection to my computer. after updating my video card driver (an old xp nvidia graphics card) so i could run the widescreen 1366 x 768 resolution, it came right up and looks very nice. it's definitely no worse than the 20" lcd lg monitor that this tv/monitor replaced.

i can highly recommend this tv since it's so cheap. if it was way over $100, no, but if you need an inexpensive tv or monitor, i think it's just fine!
summary: surprised with how good this tv is for the price

i wanted this tv for a room where i have a computer and some ham radio equipment, so i wanted this tv to double as a monitor for that computer. after attaching the base (4 screws that are included to attach the vertical part to the base, then 3 screws to attach the entire base to the tv), i plugged it in and plugged an antenna into it (antenna is not included). for an inside antenna, i picked up a lot of channels, so the tv tuner is really pretty good at picking up signals that have decent strength.

for some reason i can't adjust the tint - the tint slider is greyed out - but right out of the box the picture looks pretty decent and doesn't need tint adjustment. i did have to back off the color a few notches, but i'm pleased with the picture on this seiki!

next i got a computer monitor cable (also not included) and connected the vga connection to my computer. after updating my video card driver (an old xp nvidia graphics card) so i could run the widescreen 1366 x 768 resolution, it came right up and looks very nice. it's definitely no worse than the 20" lcd lg monitor that this tv/monitor replaced.

i can highly recommend this tv since it's so cheap. if it was way over $100, no, but if you need an inexpensive tv or monitor, i think it's just fine! surprised with how good this tv is for the price

i purchased this toshiba unit on december 18th and connected it up on december 20th. from the first movie put into the unit i started experiencing the intermittent "freezing" of the screen during playback. i tried about ten difference retail dvds and every single one of them did the freeze thing at least once. toshiba tech support took my info and had me "reset" the unit by unplugging the power for a few minutes then plug it back in. after that, the playback still intermittently freezes. toshiba tech support says that they can set up for a replacement for me, but that would involve being without a dvd player while i send it in (they won't do advance replacement) so that is out of the question. i am going to take it back to the store where i bought it and exchange it locally first. on the plus side the unit i have, manufactured in october 2006, i did not have to connect with component first to get the hdmi to work. i just plugged in the hdmi and it was working.

pros: good quality picture, lots of features (upconverting and divx) at a small price. good looking unit.

cons: the divx playback works on most things i threw at it, but not as many as my cheap $49 rca player which will play darn near anything. the picture freezing up during dvd playback is unacceptable at any price. lack of a function where a disc will start playing at the same spot as you last stopped playback.

i would say to steer away from this player at this point in time. too many issues with the playback.
summary: good picture when working, but freezing is the dealbreaker

reviewText:
since i was an early adopter and audiophile many years ago, i "invested" in large projection tvs  and state of the art home theater systems.  "state of the art" meant lots of clean power pumped through high-end speakers in a 5.0 configuration with dobly and thx certification.  the audio equipment took up a lot of room, was difficult to hook up properly for best sound dispersion, and the speakers were large and seemed to be everywhere. did i mention all the wires and cables?

but the over-riding concern became my wife's lack of approval, not just because of the space taken up and the basic institutional look, but because she had trouble turning everything on and off.  multiply that by the three systems we have and she was pretty frustrated most of the time.  when our latest tv needed upgrading i had a local guy come and hook it up.  the first thing he did was to eliminate about half the cables--but it still took him about three hours to hook up the whole system.

i took the older tv downstairs and was quoted another $250.00 to hook it up to that home theater system.  so i stopped to think about it and decided to visit a big box store and check out some of the soundbars i had researched.  this one in particular stood out because of the positive reviews, the low profile, and the cost/value comparison.  so i took it home and hooked it up.  surprisingly it was pretty simple.  the soundbar and subwoofer were already linked at the factory, so it was just a matter of hooking up the two hdmi cables:  hdmi 'out' from the cable box to hdmi 'in' on the soundbar, then hdmi 'out' from the soundbar to hdmi 'in' on the tv.  plug in both the soundbar and the subwoofer, call up the hdmi input on the remote, and you're good to go.

this is hooked up to an older samsung led tv so the pairing was easy.  the sound is so much, much  better than from the speakers in the tv.  in fact, even with the loss of half of my hearing, i couldn't turn up the volume all the way before it generated way too much sound.  the soundbar is unobtrusive, there are only two cables involved,  and the sub can be placed out of sight.  it is so much simpler than the old home theater system it replaced and my ears can no longer appreciate the nuances of such an expensive system anyway.  i'm guessing that there are a few of you out there with the same problem. nothing like the good old 60's.

my wife is impressed and happy.  it not only looks better, but you have to really look to see the soundbar  on the black tv stand.  she didn't even know that there was a sub until i showed her.  so we're both impressed with this unit.  evidently the new system replacing it  has a fancier trim and better bluetooth, but if you can pick up one of these older models you will save quite a bit of money over the new one.  highly recommended by an old audiophile.
summary: if a man says he will fix it, he will. there's no reason to remind him every six months.
