reviewText:
i think the ratings for this thing have been inflated by a bunch of bogus reviews, particularly a bunch on 1/28, probably by employees of the company or something.

not crazy about this speaker, ended up returning it.  the sound is decent but does not go very loud.  no bass to speak of but i really wasn't expecting any.  the main problem is that it cuts out once i get more than 10 feet away from it, if that.  this is a deal breaker since it defeats the whole point of being wireless/bluetooth.  i purchased this along with some other speakers to try them out and they do not cut out, so i know it's this speaker and not my phone's connection.  there are much better options out there.

the rundown:

just tried a bunch of these ranging from $20-$60:

hmdx jam bluetooth - third place - sounds awesome, it's the loudest of all tested as well. great bass and does not distort much even at the loudest volume. nice, solid weight.  however a constant buzzing/fuzzy noise made this a no go. would be my second favorite if it didn't have the buzz. well priced at 35.

satechi bluetooth audio cube - not loud at all, tinny sound, very little bass, sounds muffled. expected more from the large size of the unit(about 3.5*3.5") compared to others, and the positive reviews. looks cool.  overpriced at 50 for sure.

kinivo wired - not very loud but otherwise great sound. nice bass, clear highs.  distorts a little at max volume. cool looking.  great value at 20

sharkk bluetooth - second place - a best buy at 27 bucks. sounds great, great bass, and not much distortion on max volume. not quite as loud as the jbl or hmdx.  bland looking.  comparable volume to most of the others though.

jbl micro bluetooth - my favorite - first place. stylish, great volume, clear highs and good bass. very user friendly and uses a manual volume dial so each time you turn it on it is at the previous volume. most reset to 50% every time you turn them off and back on. bluetooth connectivity through walls is not quite as strong as others, the only con. also can be used as a bluetooth adaptor/dongle which usually costs as much as this speaker alone. the 3.5mm out can plug into any home theater system.  nice spot to hang it up on a nail, making the sound project farther and louder. also has a small flat area on the side opposite the hook so it stands up by itself.  it doesn't fall over even at max volume with bass heavy rap playing, meaning you can aim the speaker.  this actually makes the speaker louder than the hmdx for actual usage.  with extremely heavy bass music the mids and highs "fade out" a little bit at max volume since a single driver can only handle a certain amount of range.  otherwise it does not distort even at max volume.  pricey at 60 but worth it.  great battery life too, more than the advertised 5 hours.

august bluetooth - decent quality and bass, however distorts at fairly low volumes making it a no go.  similar to the sharkk in size, weight and sound.

satechi bt wireless portable speaker - worst of all, distorts at the slightest bit of bass or volume. instant no go and a rip off at 40 bucks. can also be used as a bluetooth dongle like the jbl though. looks almost identical to the kinivo.  has horrible buttons that perform multiple functions and are super sensitive leading accidental skipping of songs, turning off, etc.  stay away from satechi.

xmini - bluetooth drops easily. by far the lightest and smallest and has good sound for it's size but little bass and not too loud.  if you want portability and lightweight this is the way to go. the alpatronix is small too but heavier.  pricey at 40 for what you get.

alpatronix bluetooth - sounds great, but distorts quickly with any bass heavy music.  also "walks" across the table with bass heavy songs unlike the others due to it's weight/bass ratio.  loud, like the jbl and hdmx.  40 bucks is too much unless you don't listen to anything but classical at low volumes.

reviewText: i really wanted to love the pebble smart watch.  from the moment i began to familiarize myself with its functions and benefits, i was hopeful it would be a great introduction into the world of smart watches.  as a little more than a week of trials and errors...(a lot of errors) i decided to return the pebble watch.  the pros - good battery life, readable screen in daylight, comfortable fit.  the cons - syncing/pairing was a pain.  it seemed that i was spending at least a half hour a day trying to get it to pair/sync with my iphone 6. some of the apps were buggy, delayed or just didn't work as expected.  notifications were also streaky.  i would get some texts, some incoming call alters, but emails were never consistent.  and when they come in, they were so hard to read based on the font size.  at night the ambient auto light was just not powerful enough for me to read the messages.  by the end of my trial, i realized i was spending way too much time trying to reset, re-pair, or reinstall apps that weren't functioning.  i really wanted this to be a great fit and watch...but the fonts are too small, the screen has odd reflective properties and syncing...sinked it.  pebble seems like a great company...but i never did hear back from their support department when pairing and re-pairing became a bi-hourly issue.
summary: pebble watch - more cons than pros for my liking.

reviewText:
i am a recovering audiophile with a 15" servo velodyne that i have enjoyed for years, so i went straight to velodyne for my new sub which was to be used in a bedroom/office area which is where i spend about 2/3 of my life.  it is not for a home theater.  i chose this as i wanted something high quality, but not wanting to spend thousands on the higher-end models which, imo, are also freakishly ugly.

unfortunately, i don't know if mine was defective or just a defective design, but at low volumes (like say background music or romantic listening levels to classical/jazz), it would just cut out and have no bass at all.  if you are likely using crossed-over satellites via the included functionality or that in your amp, it is worse than no subwoofer at all.  there are only the tinny sounds from the satellites.  now, at higher bass-thumping levels, the bass is excellent, but for me having it cut out at low volumes was a deal-breaker.  the worst is at levels where you are right on the edge.  then, you'll have periods of tinny music, then switch to bass thumping, then shut off back and forth during a song.  seriously annoying!  i have never experienced this kind of behavior, even in the multitudes of the cheapest audio equipment (such as that for pcs) that i have ever owned.

this has nothing to do with the auto standby power which was also a function that didn't work.  whether on or on/off in auto standby, the "idle" power draw is the same at 11.5w.  about the only difference is the led display turns off which allegedly you can do by the remote.  this product is made in china, and i have nothing against products made in china if they are under good quality control.  there are elements of cheapness, however, such as the power cord, while being only a 2-wire cord, is the thickest, stiffest, cheapest power cord i have ever seen.  trying to straighten it out for a tidy appearance literally pulls it out from the socket in the back of the cabinet.  luckily, it also fits any cheap 2-wire or 3-wire pc power cord.

in all, this does not measure up to the previous quality of velodyne or to its current competitors that are cheaper.  combined with the defects or functional problems, i cannot recommend this product.  very disappointed.
summary: doesn't work at low volumes = fail.

i got my nook wi-fi/3g about 2 months ago, and i love it!  i researched alot of ereaders before making the decision to buy the nook; in fact, i originally bought a kindle from a local store, but never took it out of the box, and returned it to purchase the nook.

i originally decided to go with the 3g for two reasons; 1) i wasn't sure i could set up my home wi-fi to work with the nook, and 2) i wanted to be able to purchase books from absolutely anywhere.  and i've been glad i chose that; i have yet to purchase a book over just the wi-fi.  i was at a doctors office recently, waiting and waiting and waiting, and it was wonderful to be able to shop, buy a book, and start it while enduring the endless waiting.

the customer service from barnes and noble is great, all i have to do is walk in the store with my nook and the employees are knowledgable and helpful for helping with the nook.  also, the store nearest me has "classes" on saturday afternoons for nook/nookcolor owners, and i found that to be very helpful when i first purchased my nook.

speaking of the physical store, i also like that i can read any book for free for up to an hour a day in the store.  that gives me the opportunity to read alot more of a book than just what they provide as a "free sample" and lets me decide whether to purchase the book or not.

i've looked at the newest generation nook, which has just recently become available, and i'm glad i got my nook when i did; i like it so much better than any ereader i've looked at.  i can drop my nook in my purse, and anytime i'm stuck somewhere and want to read, i've got a whole library right there with me.  the nook is awesome!!!

i've had a range of other reflectors before (including a lot of jerry-rigged ones:  whiteboard, white cloth, mylar on a stiff surface--hey, in the field you improvise!  i was looking for a reflector that was cheap, easy to travel with and one to aim primarily at a limited target (like a face for a portrait, or light for a macro shot).  this reflector fits my needs perfectly.  i've used it on the road,it's easy to travel with.  perfect for close in light manipulation for a limited subject and it's got both white and golden surfaces.

if i was shooting group portraits or doing formal shots (bridal, prom poses) or needed to light up a room, i'd get something bigger with a stand or frame.  but to put some light on a still life (bowl of fruit) or someone's face or a branch with some water droplets...and then stuff it back into your fannypack or small carry bag--you can't beat this.

reviewText:
i got these headphones as a backup to my shure headphones that i (temporarily) misplaced.

my first experience with these headphones was to get them out of the blister pack they were stored in. getting to these headphones was like trying to break into fort knox. blister pack requiring scissors, then another layer to access the headphones, then removing tape, then wires, then wiring, and then pulling them out of their bed without breaking the wire... etymotic - take a clue from apple's out of the box experience, because your packaging is really, really irritating.

i've been listening to these phones for a few days now. once screwed into your ears they are very comfortable. and the audio quality is really superb - it's the best i've heard for this class of headphones. but when you're listening to something quiet with one instrument they lose it. the thin wires to the earbuds rub against your shirt when you move your head. because the wires are so thin?? they transmit the friction of their movement to your ears - amplified. what the ? it's very irritating, and the first time i've heard this. why the thin wires? i'm constantly afraid that i will break the wires when i use these headphones...

so i'm putting these headphones back into their very nicely provided bag, and going back to my shure headphones (now that i've found them).
summary: nice audio but poor industrial design

reviewText: first off: these headphones sound fantastic. since their debut a decade ago, they've become one of the standards against which all other headphones are compared. audiophiles describe the hd 650s as "euphonic" (as opposed to the more neutral hd 600s). i particularly love the warm, rich vocals these headphones produce. comfort-wise, these are good but not great. at 9.1 ounces, they're lighter than most audiophile headphones. but i still feel some strain on my neck and a slight pinch on my ears after extended wear, as is the case with nearly all headphones i've tried. the most comfortable headphones i've tried? the bose quietcomfort 15s, which are slightly lighter (7.4 ounces) and distribute that weight evenly around my ears. the qc15s also have modernity on their side: a single thin cable with iphone controls and in-line microphone, rather than a thick split cable with a 1/8" plug; a nice carrying case you can fit in your backpack rather than the shoebox the hd 650s come in; low impedance so that you can get plenty of volume out of an iphone. of course, comparing the hd 650s with the quietcomfort 15s is apples to oranges. these are audiophile headphones intended for use at home with an amp; the qc 15s are travel headphones, best-suited to wearing on planes and trains (where their active noise cancellation shines). but my ideal headphones would combine the lightness, comfort, and portability of the qc 15s with the rich sound of the hd 650s. as far as i can tell, those perfect headphones don't exist yet.

reviewText: i have a mac mini based media center and while looking for the right input device i experimented with the apple remote, a bluetooth cell phone, snatch for iphone/ipod touch, and using screen sharing with my macbook. all worked with varying degrees of success but i decided i needed a wireless keyboard with a built in touch pad regardless of what else i might use. i focused on the logitech dinovo mini and the adesso keyboard. although i liked the size of the dinovo i decided to go with the adesso due to it's mac compatibility and similarity in size and layout to my macbook keyboard. after a few hours of weird operation the adesso worked very nicely with the mac and i'm quite pleased. the keyboard is lightweight and is small enough to not be a tremendous eyesore in the living room. it is a bit expensive and doesn't have a really sturdy, high quality feel, but it's good enough. i have found that with the keyboard on my lap and the receiver in the back of the mini the connection was unstable with a lot of dropped keystrokes and choppy trackpad movement. i got a usb extension cable and moved the receiver higher and forward of other electronics which has improved the reliability considerably. i have tried to type as fast as i can to force it to drop a stroke but it doesn't happen any more. i do wish it had a redesign to make it more mac-like and similar to an apple keyboard. look at some of the images and you can see the 'clear' and 'delete' buttons on the lowest row of keys as well as the tiny 'command' key to the left of the space bar. removing the former two buttons and expanding the command key would be much better in my opinion. also the ugly two-button design and scroll control on the side of the touch pad is a bit awkward but being as it doesn't have a two-finger touchpad like the macbook it does help sometimes. and as other reviewers have stated, switching from rf to bluetooth would be a great improvement as well. in summation, if adesso (or another company) could make just a few tweaks to this unit to pretty it up, make it bluetooth and possibly add two-finger control but keep the price the same, it would be a fantastic mac input device. as it stands, it's pretty darn good though.
summary: it does the job nicely but could use an upgrade.

this case does what it's intended for very well.  it's light, compact and holds my nikon d80 and attached 18-200mm f/3.5-5.6 vr lens.  the build quality is excellent and the lining and padding are very nice. if you just want to carry an slr and a large zoom lens, this is the bag for you.  the price is hard to beat.

however, that said, i'm going to be looking for another bag in the near future.  i have a tamrac that holds several lenses, speedlight and an slr, but it won't hold them all with a lens mounted.  so, i was hoping this bag would be my solution to keeping a superzoom on the camera all the time.  i overlooked my desire to keep a speedlight and filters handy.  i use fill-flash a great deal of the time and this bag has no provision to carry one.  there isn't enough extra room in the main compartment for a speedlight and the small side pouch will not comfortably hold a filter-carrier.  there are no side-loops or other attachment points, just a thick belt-loop on the body-side.

i'm currently looking at the lowepro mini-mag as i think it might be the solution for my particular application.

reviewText:
the good: i have the projector in a small room, 11 1/2 feet from the wall, and it's projecting a 200" image! call it theater of the absurd, but i like that senselessly huge picture.  right now it's projecting onto my wall, with no professional material, and the picture is still superb. crisp, vibrant, and so real.  obviously i'll be getting a real screen soon to stop the color bleeding from the uneven surface.  i just watched mud in 1080p and it looked just like the movies, with that oh-so-real effect from the dlp chip.  the projector is quiet for 33db, i don't notice it on because my stereo conquers the noise.  obviously there's a lot of heat coming from it, but this is normal for any projector. there is no motion blur whatsoever, and the contrast and black levels are superb.  there is not much light coming from the projector unlike some other ones i've seen. the picture is still overall square which some short throws i have heard of issues with. the pixels are still tiny and not noticeable except from a  very close distance.

now, onto why it gets 3 stars....

the bad: there is an issue with consistent focus across the screen, but only if you have it set to the minimal screen size setting.  the first one i got had a portion on the top left and bottom right middle that wouldn't come into complete focus, at or around 85% focus, on the smallest screen setting, creating a noticeable blur on text, and a sometimes noticeable blur in motion. when setting the screen to the completely full size, there is absolutely no problem at all with the focus consistency.  i thought this may be a quality control issue but the second one is the same way, albeit with less of an issue.  the focus all around is pretty good but on the bottom right middle its about 90% focus as compared to 100% focus, again, only with the smallest screen setting. this only occurs when the screen is set to it's minimum size. when i have it set anywhere past this the focus issue is not present.  however the room i have it in, i have to have it set to it's minimal picture size, so i don't have a choice, because i don't have a roof mount, i just have it sitting on a desk in the back of the room.  so, if you do plan on purchasing this, buy a ceiling mount, or make sure and use it as a short throw project should be used, nice and close to the wall, and you won't have any focus issue, because you'll be able to set it to it's maximum screen size.  i'm still giving 3 stars because the company shouldn't even allow the screen to get so small if it cannot remain in focus properly.

i also had the 1070 benq, which did not have any focus issue, hooked up to my same pc (macbook pro 1080p hookup, i even bought an extra adapter and hdmi cable to verify the issue's source).

overall: i still highly recommend this, but it's getting three stars from me because i"m 2/2 in bad focus on the small pic setting.  due to outstanding overall quality and every other good outweighing the bad, i  still recommend this projector.

update: i bought a roof mount and picture is perfect.  i also moved some furniture and put it on the floor in the middle of the room to see how the picture would be and it was perfect.  so, basically lesson learned is that this project doesn't like to be in the back of the room on the minimal screen size setting.  my family came over and watched a couple movies with me, and they're already bought their own!

there is a lot to like about this receiver and i agree with most of the positives as outlined by other reviewers so i won't list them. i want to however, talk about the negatives.
i keep my receiver on so it is powered up when i turn the ignition on. there are times though when the receiver just shuts down itself and there are also times when i have to reset all the information such as date, time and other settings.
i have a sd card inserted. the receiver almost always default to it when it is powered up no matter what other source it was on when it was shut down.
it inserts gaps in my cd mixes even though they were recorded without.
the receiver does not have the rear camera guides built in. i hooked it up to the factory installed rear camera and while i can see what's behind me, there are no lines to guide me.
i agree with other reviewers that there should be a subwoofer level control.
the issues listed above i find annoying. i don't think i will purchase this brand again unless they fix them.
summary: not bad but a number of issues

based on past experience with cables to go, the junk i received is not their product, but a super cheap knock-off.  beware this vendor - this is not legitimate stuff.
summary: this is not a cables to go cable - do not buy marginmart cables!!

reviewText:
the hp 318 was my first digital camera purchase and it was an absolute failure.  despite using kodaks at work, i was lured by the lower price on the hp unit.  that was a mistake because as a professional photographer pointed out to me afterwards, computer companies generally don't make good cameras.  right away, my hp 318 went through batteries like there was no tomorrow.  at first, i thought it was just a power-hungry unit (it does take 4 aa batteries, after all).  one evening, i took out the camera and got some photos of a nice sunset and then came back indoors.  instead of putting the camera away, i set it on my desk and noticed that the flash was firing intermittently. i checked and yes, the camera was turned off yet the red-eye reduction flash was firing. that explained the multitude of dead batteries. i removed the batteries and the flash kept going off for at least fifteen more minutes, possibly longer as the capacitors bled off their charge. i placed the unit back in the box and returned it the next day.  i got a kodak dx-3500 and have been very satisfied with it.
okay, anybody could get a defective camera. this is what else i found wrong with the hp 318:
* focus - this camera has a weird focus. even though the manual says it will focus on the center object in the viewfinder, if there is anything else in the frame with greater contrast, the camera focuses on it instead of your intended subject.
* flimsy - the camera is made primarily of lightweight plastic and it feels like cheap lightweight plastic. the wrist strap partially obstructs the compact flash door on the side. the battery compartment lid works itself loose with normal camera use. the camera is too small for adult hands. there is no lens cap. there are no indicator lines in the viewfinder to tell you where the edges of your photograph lie.
* picture quality - all pictures from this camera seemed overexposed. to get proper color balance, i had to use a graphics program to adjust color levels and hsb.
for a few more dollars, you can get a much better camera.

reviewText: i was excited to get such an inexpensive bag. reviews were great, anything by amazon basics is great (cables, cases, etc.). i wanted a bulkier bag for my dslr, ultrabook, and gopro/mounts for when we travel. the bag itself is very nice, high quality, lots of pockets and space. one major flaw for me that is an absolute deal breaker is the partition setup for the dslr/lenses. the partitions are removable so that the user can move them around to allow for maximum storage around any side/dimension of lens or other accessory. the problem with this is using velcro as it doesn't hold together well at all. i thought "meh, when the velcro wears out, i'll just discard the bag." the issue though is when the bag shifts, the partitions pull against one another and then you basically just have a padded partition unattached, but still possibly separating your equipment. it's not a horrible product, but i would rather give up the convenience of moving partitions around for some sewn in pieces or at least something more stable but still removable. basic plastic clips attached to the partitions that you could slide or snap together would allow for that, but not separate/wear out as easy as velcro.

i always thought bose to be overpriced and "trendy", more for people with more money than common sense. then we got the bose cinemate 1 sr digital home theater speaker system for our bedroom big screen. everything i thought i knew went out the window at that instant. i would begin this review with the build quality. i rail against china constantly. yet these are made in china....but as someone in china once told me, "you ask for cheap, we build you cheap, you want quality, we build quality. you pay for what you get". these bose speakers just reflect what he said that day as i find the build quality exceptionally nice. i find the sound exceptionally nice.

  thanks to war, aging and a wife screaming at me for too long, i now wear hearing aids. since that day i really have struggled to find ways to recover frequencies now dead to me. these speakers do that for me. for all i do except gaming, i now use these. especially music. in my home as well as dragging them out to my hot tub. they sound that clear to me. to be able to distinguish different instruments & vocals clearly is something that has eluded me the past year or so, so it is a really big deal for me. i honestly love how much sound, clear sound i can pull in from these speakers. unlike some who find them with too much bass, i do not. i also use my settings in windows to adjust the bass , treble and other sound "effects" to my liking and compensate where and if i need to.

  the wiring.....i ding this 1 full star for the wiring. while some with compact needs may be thrilled with the short wires, i need to spend money to buy extension wiring for 3 of the ways i use these. for the list price i find that offensive. no excuse on earth to me that they do this. if nothing else, i would suggest to bose they add a little wiring extension kit to supplement the standard wiring as an option for someone who needs that extra length. i love these so much i drag them around for several different uses as mentioned earlier and simply can't even use them without that extra 2 feet of wire. another reason to remove that 1 full star is the list price. while i give these 10 stars (if i could) for sound alone, i only paid eighty bucks for a new set of logitech x-540 5.1 surround sound speaker system with subwoofer here at amazon. they sound amazing as well and look at how much more you get. also, i have 3 years of hardcore gaming into them and they are good as new. one other little nitpick is i wish there were a treble & bass adjustment on the speakers to make it easier to adjust without the need to use windows 8 sound settings.

  so i leave this with 4 stars, well earned. now to that radio shack for the wire extension i have to buy.

  the wiring.....i ding this 1 full star for the wiring. while some with compact needs may be thrilled with the short wires, i need to spend money to buy extension wiring for 3 of the ways i use these. for the list price i find that offensive. no excuse on earth to me that they do this. if nothing else, i would suggest to bose they add a little wiring extension kit to supplement the standard wiring as an option for someone who needs that extra length. i love these so much i drag them around for several different uses as mentioned earlier and simply can't even use them without that extra 2 feet of wire. another reason to remove that 1 full star is the list price. while i give these 10 stars (if i could) for sound alone, i only paid eighty bucks for a new set of logitech x-540 5.1 surround sound speaker system with subwoofer here at amazon. they sound amazing as well and look at how much more you get. also, i have 3 years of hardcore gaming into them and they are good as new. one other little nitpick is i wish there were a treble & bass adjustment on the speakers to make it easier to adjust without the need to use windows 8 sound settings.

reviewText:
i wanted my husband to mount this to the doorframe but we ended up just keeping it loose, which i would say is one of its best features: you don't *have* to use it outside. it came in handy when my husband had dental surgery and fell asleep on the couch. i couldn't sit by him all day, so i put the camera next to the sofa so he could call me when he needed something. this could possibly be useful to parents with children playing outside, too, but i didn't test its range.

the camera works well enough but there's quite a noticeable lag time, which could be an issue if you have it outside and your visitors keep moving around. i would not consider this a good value for the money, and as others have noted, it feels quite cheap. still, there are times when a built-in camera isn't desirable, and the fact that you can move this around easily is a  plus.

there is no volume control and the "bell" is this horrid screech that sounds like something out of a horror movie. even knowing this, i nearly jumped out of my chair when my husband pushed the bell to call me. for the price this should have a volume control, and maybe a choice of tones. at least put a pleasant chime on the thing!

if you don't want to install a high-end door intercom or you have a need to occasionally move the camera unit around, this could fit the bill. it works well enough to be useful, but the functionality is bare-bones. if you don't jump from electronic bleeps then you won't mind its squawking. i don't know if i'll get around to putting this outside, since i don't get a lot of visitors, but putting the camera unit in the basement and keeping the receiver in my upstairs office might be useful. however, i wasn't able to initiate calls from the receiver so this limits its usefulness for two-way communications.

reviewText:
i've tested two d5200's (one from amazon, another from bh) and they've both been consistently back focusing with the several lenses i have tried.  back focusing (the camera and/or lens focuses slightly farther than where you target) seems to be an epidemic problem among both canon and nikon slr cameras.  it is a frequent cause of soft images.  this purchase has been very frustrating, because it is an otherwise wonderful camera.  a salesman told me that many photographers end up exchanging several times before getting a keeper. this seems like a ridiculous technological disparity--they've got a sensor that can capture an ingrown hair on a gnat's left buttock but the camera won't focus properly.  i was told that it's very hard to callibrate a camera to be accurate with all the lenses that are available....but if the problem is back focusing 90% of the time (which seems to be the case with numerous models--i've never heard of a problem with front focusing) why don't these guys start adjusting their products to compensate for that?
update
after shooting hundreds of test pics and comparing with the d7100 i've concluded that i was getting my drawers in a buch over nothing. the back focusing only seems to be a problem with extreme macro photography; the 1/8 inch inaccuracy does not interfere with sharpness under normal shooting conditions. although the d7100 is slightly more accurate wide open at very close range, when taking a picture of a person at f/8 from across the room the sharpness is exacatly the same. the resolution really is incredible, and the detail you can extract from the shadows is unlike any dslr i've ever seen.
summary: back focuses slightly but otherwise fantastic camera

reviewText:
my first every ebay score, the canon ef-s 17-85mm lens (featuring image stabilization) was a much coveted item around here.  it had come highly recommended and seemed to be a great complement to my beloved 50mm prime and a perfect replacement for the 18-55mm kit lens that shipped with the xti.

initial, first-night impressions?  heavenly.

compared to the other lenses that i've put on the business end of the xti, the 17-85mm is one heavy dude.  i'd wager that it's at least as heavy as the camera and certainly feels as heavy as the 50mm and the 18-55mm put together.  the lens is serious.  it means business.  it traveled back in time from the future to be here with us today.  it's a touch of the photographic high-tech, made accessible to the amateur.

with my right hand on the shutter and my left on the lens' barrel, it didn't feel any less heavy but "heavy", in my mind, became "solid".  the auto-focus is nice and quiet and is reasonably fast to lock onto the subject.  the focusing ring is also nice and big -- it cries out to be grasped and twisted.  it was a joy to realize that even with the auto-focus turned on, the lens would not complain if i fine-tuned a given shot with some manual adjustments.  (the af doesn't totally commandeer the focus, that is to say.)  the zoom is also smooth, the barrel moving quickly and easily without over-shooting the desired focal length.

image stabilization is also a big plus.  i have a feeling that once i get the hang of it, it will save quite a few low-light, indoor, and hand-held shots over the lifetime of this lens.  this isn't to be nave and believe it to be a cure-all.  certainly a few of my early test shots with the is feature on prove that you can still wind up with a whole mess of blur.  but others worked out pretty well.

after having used it for about two weeks or so now, most of these initial impressions have stayed true.  the is feature is a good one but isn't something upon which to rely to save every shot.  you still need to have good light and the right angle, etc.; but with the right iso setting, it can save the scene.  the heavy feeling of the lens is something i've gotten used to pretty quickly; after a couple of sessions, you just expect the camera to weight that much -- no worries.  i've also found that the longer focal lengths are great for portraiture -- i find myself using focal lengths in the 70-85mm range pretty often now and i wonder how i ever lived without them before.

that said, i'm beginning to wonder a little about the lens' chromatic aberration.  i've had a few shots that don't seem to "resolve" the same way during post-processing (in aperture) as similar shots under similar conditions with the same camera body and a different lens (e.g., the 50mm prime).  this is not to say that i have my mind made up and am squaring the blame on the lens -- certainly not!  but i am trying to parse my way through some of these, experimenting with some different conditions, etc. to see where it lands.  i've just fallen into a certain rhythm with my post-processing and i would hate to have to learn a new dance just for the one, new lens.

all things considered however, i've been very pleased with most of my results from the 17-85mm thus far.

...so yeah, worth it.

but with respect to "worth it":  canon lists a retail price of $600 for the ef-s 17-85mm is lens.  most places online seem to offer it in the $475-$550 range.  as far as lenses go, this is hardly a costly one.  considering that this is one of the two lenses "given away" as the kit lens for canon's 40d body, you wonder a little bit if the mass-production maybe watered it down just a little bit...?  just the same, this is a great "walk-around" lens:  it is sturdy, has some great built-in features, and has a versatile range of focal lengths.  if you got this lens "free" with your camera body then you are in luck.  if you're looking to pick up one separately...  well, it's a great lens to have.  and i'm happy with mine.  but see if you can't score one on ebay or through your local re-seller of high-quality, previously enjoyed lenses.

happy shooting, y'all.
summary: great walk-around lens (maybe some chromatic aberration?)

reviewText: so, we decided to "unplug" about a year ago and rely on a combination of amazon prime instant video, hulu plus, and traditional broadcast for our tv viewing needs. all in all it's been great. we have small children and they are perfectly content with the programming options available. the price difference between paying for cable/satellite on a monthly basis is fantastic. we purchased this antenna a few months back and i have to say that the reception is spotty at best. despite the "amplified" signal, we are constantly dealing with the audio cutting in and out while watching tv. it's very frustrating. also, if we do not have the antenna in the absolute perfect spot, we get a very weak signal, and have to move the antenna all together if we even want to be able to watch certain channels. granted, some of this is definitely due to our proximity to the local broadcasting stations. we are not in a rural location by any means though, so the signal quality should be good. the strangest part is that when i open the signal meter in the tv options, the signal is sometimes as high as 100%, yet we experience breaks in audio and digital "static" at the same time. we watch broadcast tv so rarely that it has not been enough of an issue to switch back to cable/satellite, but it's still very frustrating when we do try and watch a local channel.

i have my a610 a week now after having owned two digital cameras.  the last camera was a canon a10 so this camera is a vast improvement.  i love this camera!  the pictures are wonderfully clear and crisp.  my only negative comment is that it is a little tricky getting a good focus and exposure at macro settings. this thing will focus down to 1 cm! i found it best not to use the flash on close up shots as it tends over expose. the manual tells you this and a good exposure is possible with just a minimal amount of light without the flash.

  the menus are straight forward but complex.  canon has allowed settings for just about everything. i can't imagine a setting that was missed.

 the camera is slightly on the large size and a little heavy since it has 4 batteries, but it runs forever on that power source.  the extra space needed for the batteries gives the camera  a nice grip since the front protrudes out allowing you to hold the camera very still for low light settings.

  i like the finish on the camera contrary to previous complaints.  it is a textured silver finish rather than gloss and, i guess, it all a matter of taste.  i do not think it has a cheap finish. besides, the fit or the various pieces are almost perfect.  this should not discourage you from buying this camera. actually, i would have preferred an all black camera anyway, but silver seems to be the rage these days.

  it has wonderful low light capabilities which are better than my old 35mm slr.  i was really surprised about this.  i have noticed no noise problems in really low light.

  the mechanical mechanisms are quiet and sound very refined.  my old camera was rough and noisy.

  we looked at a lot of cameras an did a great deal of research.  i am very satisfied with this purchase and highly recommend it.

reviewText:
i had a sony bdp-s590 3d blu-ray player, but my big puppy jumped on me and i fell hitting the open disc tray with my shoulder. i tried opening up the unit to see if it was something i could fix; unfortunately, i found a large white gear broken in half. the bdp s590 was history. in the process, i had also discovered that the sony bdp-s590 was built like crap. its innards are just cheap.

i had paid less than $100 for the quite good performing bdp-s590, so i took a chance on its successor the bdp-s5100; i have not been disappointed. the bdp-s5100 is even faster than the bdp-s590. blu-ray discs load immediately. the blu-ray picture is excellent with incredible detail, very low digital noise, and good color . dvds also look very good with upscaling to 1080p; it's actually the best i have seen yet in this price range. 3d blu-rays look great too. titanic 3d, dredd 3d, pacific rim, and promethius 3d all look fantastic with this player.

another plus with the sony is that it has both  optical and digital coaxial sound outputs. i have the digital coaxial connected to a multiple input and output digital coaxial switch and selector. that way i get dolby digital and dts 5.1 sent to my 3 older jvc digital receivers with digital soundfield processing.  unfortunately, they don't have hdmi inputs and outputs, but thanks to their digital coaxial inputs, i still get dolby digital and dts 5.1 96/24 audio output to my 5.1 x 3 surround setup with dual 10" subs.

disappointingly, the bdp-s5100 is just as unsubstantial as my older bdp-s590. this is definitely not going to be a long lived device. at 2 pounds it is light as a feather which smacks of cheapness. like the bdp-s590 it is likely the same: all delicate plastic, very thin stamped steel, and small misplaced globs of grease. however, the bdp-s5100s saving grace is its superb blu-ray processing .

meanwhile, i will not be letting this player connect to the internet most of the time. unfortunately, sony forces firmware updates that enforce more and more restrictive "features" on the user. as a result, i will connect to let it do firmware updates only after i read about their effects from those that have a given version. i am just using the bdp-s5100 as my workhorse blu-ray player for all the movies i rent from redbox and netflix.  it's a great performer when used as such. its 2d to 3d conversion actually works ok on a few titles. i use my smart 3d wi-fi hdtv for streaming.

finally, the bdp-s5100s quasi-pyramid/stealth-bomber top is just ridiculous in my opinion.  amazingly, all the main blu-ray player makers are following this same silly "artsy" design philosophy with weird shapes and all the buttons on the top. it's as if they think owners are going to have their $100 player on a special display table in front of their big screen 3d smart hdtvs for everyone to marvel at- just silly. all my components are in dust protected cabinets with shelves, but i won't be stacking anything on top of the sony due to its shape. luckily the buttons on top are raised, and there are only four. sony, please put the control buttons back on the front where they belong. you're not the only component i own, so why not play nice with the others.
summary: fine as my workhorse 3d blu-ray player only

reviewText:
this is an easy-to-use and easy-to-install device aimed at extending your wireless signal farther than your router can reach. the basic idea is that you set it up so that it gets signal from your router, and then you can place it somewhere at a distance from your router and connect your computer to the wireless signal emanating from it.

it's easy to set up - just plug it in somewhere near to your main router, and then hook it up to your computer via the included ethernet cable. you'll see the wireless signal with "edimax" in the name, and connect to that. then go to the website "http://edimax. setup" and follow directions. you'll need to have the password to your wireless access point(s) handy, and select which of them you want the device to pick up. (with some routers it's even easier: just push a button on the router and then a button on the extender and they connect automatically.)

once it's set up, you can place it anywhere you like, as long as it can pick up a signal from the original router. then, if you connect to this device (it appears on my list of wireless access points under the name of my original access point with a "_2ex" on the end).

what it does is spread the signal farther than it would normally extend. that could be a very good thing in a large office or house - i've got a fairly small house that gets signal throughout, but it can be weak in places far away from the router, like my bedroom, for example. so i placed it in my bedroom and it really does boost the signal strength quite a bit.

what it doesn't do is boost the speed - in fact it slows things down. a speed test showed that in the same spot, with my regular hotspot i was able to download 28mbps; with the extender i could only get 18mbps. it doesn't make much of a difference for casual browsing, but it can hurt the quality of video streaming, so it's really a tradeoff in terms of getting a boosted signal farther away, but it's not as fast as it would be anywhere you could get a decent signal.

overall, this is a useful device that could be helpful for some purposes - especially where you want to extend the signal in a large space; but the speed loss does make it less useful than i'd hoped it would be. (note: i was given a sample of this device by the manufacturer for the purpose of testing and review.)
summary: this easy-to-use device does extend and strengthen wireless signals - but it doesn't maintain download and upload speed

reviewText:
i don't know why i had higher expectations for this but my experience with this adapter leaves me with mixed feelings. while i didn't expect the fastest 802.11ac card on the market, i find myself disappointed by wifi yet again. i went out and bought a nice new ubiquiti ac lite access point, was really impressed with the range and decided "maybe wireless is finally a contender for home use compared to wired", i mean 802.11ac touts up to 1300mbps speeds! i didn't expect 1300mbps or even 650mbps from a sub-$200 setup, i was disappointed to see speeds of under 100mbps also. the stability is getting better, but it's still not there for me either.

performance

so on to performance. i installed the card into the pcie 2.0 x1 slot (i tried both on my motherboard to see if there was any performance difference from irqs or anything like that and there wasn't), then installed the latest driver my pc could find (18.33.3.2) and also downloaded the drivers on asus's website for windows 10 64bit (18.20.0.9), then disabled my onboard nic to start playing with the wireless. after a few reboots to ensure everything was stable, i ran some iperf tests using the latest driver but all results were under 70mbps even with the antenna sitting on top of the access point on my desk. i uninstalled the latest driver, switched to the asus driver, and rebooted my pc (this was required for the best results). with the antenna sitting on the wireless access point i was seeing upwards of 200mbps, still depressingly slow compared to wired but it's a start. i moved my access point back to my closet about 20 feet away with 2 cement walls between the antenna and access point, and iperf is reporting the following:

_iperf over udp_
86.5mbps upload
71.3mbps download

_iperf over tcp_
53.3mbps upload
52.0mbps download

now how does this translate to wan speeds? unfortunately not so good, i'm unable to hit the 50mbps up or down that my internet package supports while the access point is in a different room. here are the results using speedtest:

_speedtest over wireless_
latency 14ms
28.65mbps download
32.41mbps upload

_speedtest over wired_
latency 12ms
58.41mbps download
65.76mbps upload

stability

so performance aside, let's take a look at stability. connectivity is solid even with 2 concrete walls between the antenna and access point, no drops and windows is reporting at least 120mbps speed (tests beg to differ but at least we know it's using ac over n) with 4 out of 5 bars of signal quality. unfortunately the latency is all over the board as is common with wireless, pings to my local server would start off normal with ~1ms of latency but then jump up to over 200ms after less than 10 pings. i ran winmtr for 50 packets and it shows an average latency of 30ms with the best being 1ms and the worst being 223ms. 223ms is fine for browsing websites and checking e-mail but 223ms is really bad when it comes to any kind of streaming content (i.e. video, voip, online gaming, etc...). we're talking milliseconds here but if the latency is constantly hitting just over 200ms every 10 pings or so it may be noticeable depending on your application. i honestly doubt this issue is specific to this make or model of wireless adapter but it's worth pointing out since people just look at speeds and don't consider other factors like latency which has a better impact than speed when you're comparing 10/100 wired vs 802.11ac wireless.

results

my conclusion is that these wireless cards are decent for the price, especially when you consider they have built in bluetooth if you attach it to a usb header (i have not tested this). i ordered 3 of them based on reviews and don't plan on returning or replacing them but it will be a while before i consider switching from wired to wireless. i do plan on purchasing a much more expensive 802.11ac pci card and an ubiquiti ac pro access point (for the 3x3 antenna and 802.3af compatibility) to play with to see how performance is impacted compared to this pci card, but i doubt anything will sway me from my wired connection anytime soon. running wires in my house isn't exactly easy though so some rooms would benefit from these wireless cards, i just don't think i'll be reducing my wired devices like i was hoping to though.
summary: not bad, but not great either.

reviewText:
comparing startech to buffalo:

i recently purchased and returned a buffalo print server, so i'll begin this review with a short comparison. the buffalo had only a small documentation insert, maybe 10 palm sized pages. the startech server includes a quick start guide of the same length, but also on their install cd is a 146 page document with detailed user instructions.  the buffalo instructions are either consistently wrong and/or misleading while the startech instructions are clear and accurate.  the startech user manual was written by a non-native american english speaker, but the occasional inelegant phrasing is a small price to pay for the information.  the startech install cd works and all links to documentation and software work--the buffalo cd does not work as documented and links to the documentation are broken.  the most important difference for me is that on the buffalo print server a 16 page 11mb file caused the server to fail and print only the first 2 pages with either blanks or garbage filed pages following.  the same document prints perfectly through the startech unit.

both units have web-base administration options, but the startech is more cleanly designed and offers many more features.  the startech manual includes instructions on firmware upgrades, which i have not yet tried. the buffalo print server instructions and web site offer nothing in the way of firmware upgrades.

i have owned the startech unit for only 24 hours, so there may be updates to this review should anything important develop in the future.

hardware setup:

my hardware setup is a dell desktop dimension xps gen3 with 3tb of storage and dual lcd monitors, an hp laserjet p2015d printer, a dell laptop and a linksys wireless wrt54g-tm router which was supplied by t-mobile. the laptop is connected wirelessly to the router, the desktop is wired directly via an ethernet cable. both computers run windows xp sp3.

installation of the print server:

the package description does not mention the need for an ethernet cable to connect the server and the router, but you will need to purchase one if you don't have a spare lying around as i was lucky enough to have.

i performed the initial installation on the desktop and used the default settings with two exceptions. i used an ip address of 192.168.0.115 and i changed the default server name to "p1."  on my router, under basic setup screen, the dhcp server is enabled using a starting address of 192.168.0.100.  i limited the max users to 10 and assigned a static dns 1 as 192.168.0.115.  the desktop installation process and testing of the 16 page document took approximately 10 minutes from unpacking to printing.

installation of local printer:

the installation structuctions are a bit uncleat on the actual setting up of the local printer so i'll relate what worked for me:

click on control panel, select printers and faxes. select add printer option. select "local printer attached to this computer" and click next. on select a printer port screen select creat a new port. use the pull down to select "standard tcp/ip port. a new wizard will open up. on the add port page i typed in my static ip address 192.168.0.115. the port name is automatically filled in so go to the next page. on the additional port information required page, keep the default generic network card and click next.  now you are finished with the hard part.  just select your printer, install the drivers if needed, and print your test page.  the same procedure can be followed on any other computer, including laptops that you wish to access the server.

one note of warning.  if you cannot ping the ip address of the server from the computer you are using, installation will fail. it's beyond the scope of this review to resolve that issue, it personally took me several hours of trial and error. one useful tool is a free program called angryip.  it will automatically test for live reachable ips and for any open ports associated with them. mcafee warns prior to installing this program, but i have suffered no ill effects from using it.

internet printing:

the print server also supports ipp (printing over the internet) and you can find detailed instructions in their user manual. again using the add printer in windows xp, just select "a network printer, or a printer attached to another computer and on the specify a printer page click connect to a printer on the internet or a home or office network.  i then typed in :"[...]" (without the quotes).  now if i happen to have my laptop in an internet cafe and feel the urge to print, ill have it waiting when i get home. it did feel a bit strange using the lpt1 for the install, however it worked on the first try so who am i to get upset?  just follow the instructions in the manual, substituting your own ip address, and if needed your forwarding port if you use something other than the standard.

one additional installation note for internet printing to work.  you'll need to go to your router and setup port forwarding.  on my linksys i went to the applications and gaming area, typed in ipp for the application name, 631 for the starting and ending port range, selected tcp as the protocol, typed in 115 as the ending part of the preselect ipaddress and checked enable. then saved the settings. you may need to make firewall changes and possibly on the router uncheck the block anonymous internet requests on the security tab area. internet printing is dead easy once installed.

conclusion:

if the need for an ethernet cable had been mentioned and if the documentation for adding printers had been just a little more clear it would have rated 5 stars.

overall, the startech device seems to be a good bargain for $45.00.  i'd purchase another one and would recommend it to anyone in the market for a good, cheap, well-documented unit that works.
summary: good, inexpensive, well documented unit that works

comparing startech to buffalo:

i recently purchased and returned a buffalo print server, so i'll begin this review with a short comparison. the buffalo had only a small documentation insert, maybe 10 palm sized pages. the startech server includes a quick start guide of the same length, but also on their install cd is a 146 page document with detailed user instructions.  the buffalo instructions are either consistently wrong and/or misleading while the startech instructions are clear and accurate.  the startech user manual was written by a non-native american english speaker, but the occasional inelegant phrasing is a small price to pay for the information.  the startech install cd works and all links to documentation and software work--the buffalo cd does not work as documented and links to the documentation are broken.  the most important difference for me is that on the buffalo print server a 16 page 11mb file caused the server to fail and print only the first 2 pages with either blanks or garbage filed pages following.  the same document prints perfectly through the startech unit.

both units have web-base administration options, but the startech is more cleanly designed and offers many more features.  the startech manual includes instructions on firmware upgrades, which i have not yet tried. the buffalo print server instructions and web site offer nothing in the way of firmware upgrades.

i have owned the startech unit for only 24 hours, so there may be updates to this review should anything important develop in the future.

hardware setup:

my hardware setup is a dell desktop dimension xps gen3 with 3tb of storage and dual lcd monitors, an hp laserjet p2015d printer, a dell laptop and a linksys wireless wrt54g-tm router which was supplied by t-mobile. the laptop is connected wirelessly to the router, the desktop is wired directly via an ethernet cable. both computers run windows xp sp3.

installation of the print server:

the package description does not mention the need for an ethernet cable to connect the server and the router, but you will need to purchase one if you don't have a spare lying around as i was lucky enough to have.

i performed the initial installation on the desktop and used the default settings with two exceptions. i used an ip address of 192.168.0.115 and i changed the default server name to "p1."  on my router, under basic setup screen, the dhcp server is enabled using a starting address of 192.168.0.100.  i limited the max users to 10 and assigned a static dns 1 as 192.168.0.115.  the desktop installation process and testing of the 16 page document took approximately 10 minutes from unpacking to printing.

installation of local printer:

the installation structuctions are a bit uncleat on the actual setting up of the local printer so i'll relate what worked for me:

click on control panel, select printers and faxes. select add printer option. select "local printer attached to this computer" and click next. on select a printer port screen select creat a new port. use the pull down to select "standard tcp/ip port. a new wizard will open up. on the add port page i typed in my static ip address 192.168.0.115. the port name is automatically filled in so go to the next page. on the additional port information required page, keep the default generic network card and click next.  now you are finished with the hard part.  just select your printer, install the drivers if needed, and print your test page.  the same procedure can be followed on any other computer, including laptops that you wish to access the server.

one note of warning.  if you cannot ping the ip address of the server from the computer you are using, installation will fail. it's beyond the scope of this review to resolve that issue, it personally took me several hours of trial and error. one useful tool is a free program called angryip.  it will automatically test for live reachable ips and for any open ports associated with them. mcafee warns prior to installing this program, but i have suffered no ill effects from using it.

internet printing:

the print server also supports ipp (printing over the internet) and you can find detailed instructions in their user manual. again using the add printer in windows xp, just select "a network printer, or a printer attached to another computer and on the specify a printer page click connect to a printer on the internet or a home or office network.  i then typed in :"[...]" (without the quotes).  now if i happen to have my laptop in an internet cafe and feel the urge to print, ill have it waiting when i get home. it did feel a bit strange using the lpt1 for the install, however it worked on the first try so who am i to get upset?  just follow the instructions in the manual, substituting your own ip address, and if needed your forwarding port if you use something other than the standard.

one additional installation note for internet printing to work.  you'll need to go to your router and setup port forwarding.  on my linksys i went to the applications and gaming area, typed in ipp for the application name, 631 for the starting and ending port range, selected tcp as the protocol, typed in 115 as the ending part of the preselect ipaddress and checked enable. then saved the settings. you may need to make firewall changes and possibly on the router uncheck the block anonymous internet requests on the security tab area. internet printing is dead easy once installed.

conclusion:

if the need for an ethernet cable had been mentioned and if the documentation for adding printers had been just a little more clear it would have rated 5 stars.

overall, the startech device seems to be a good bargain for $45.00.  i'd purchase another one and would recommend it to anyone in the market for a good, cheap, well-documented unit that works. good, inexpensive, well documented unit that works

reviewText: an ok gps unit, but the phone/xm/bluetooth features which are premium add-ons (and the reason i bought this thing) just flat do not work reliably.  my attempts to get a cardo scala qz bluetooth headset failed miserably, after following directions, spending a ludicrous amount of time attempting resets per scala tech support.  garmin tech support could not give a list of compatible bluetooth headsets and actually suggested i try a bunch of different ones until i found one that worked.  for a unit with a list price of a grand ($999 usd, plus motorcycle mount adapter plus xm subscription plus headset costs) this puppy should be turnkey.  buyer beware; a simple gps with an alternative for listening to music while doing long distance motorcycle riding is called for as the advertised features on this pos just plain suck and waste time trying to make them work.  i will try another brand headset, we shall see, but the lack of tested gps/bluetooth headset pairs for this is inexcusable for garmin; telling customers to "try different headsets and see what works" is inexcusable and something they should have done as part of product rollout/support.
summary: bluetooth implementation & support sub-standard and inexcusable

it took a great while to get this to work, but it finally did, and it's a good thingy-dingy. it won't work with w10. it needs to have the setup disk plugged in and ran after connecting the usb cable. it needs to have the win control panel opened, and the monitor attributes tweaked, then the stuff applied, then ok'd, then the pc restarted. you will see it come up as either a "usb monitor," or as a "vga monitor" in control panel, but if it's going to work at all you will be able to first detect it, then identify it with those big white numbers.

there is no documentation to help you through this maze. the disk's release notes are cryptic, and not meant for earthpeople.  there is no rhyme or reason as to what file to choose on the install disk menu, and no readme.

but it does eventually work!
summary: a tough row to hoe, but the veggies can pop up

reviewText: the quality is great but sadly this does not fit the 15.4" macbook pro. well... actually it does fit if you want to spend a minute squeezing and stretching it in there. i have no idea how some of the other reviewers manage to be fine with this case being so tight. the unibody macbook pro is about 14.5" wide and this case is only 14" wide at the center (it tapers in). it "fits like a glove" (as another reviewer said) but a glove one size too small that you struggle to shove your hand into. maybe the other reviews are from another discontinued size of this case, since amazon has a tendency to lump product reviews of similar but not the same product together. it is so tight that it has to apply pressure to the back of the screen which isn't good. the 15" cargo sleeve is in the same boat for not fitting correctly built 15-inch cargo laptop sleeve, black. see my review of the other larger built olive case i am keeping instead: built ny medium 15" laptop case (olive). this case is the same color, same material, same handle. the strap on this one is padded in the middle (unlike the larger bag), which is a plus, and the material is soft and squishy which should protect against minor bumps and hits. it will most likely not protect your computer from being dented if you drop it from 3+ feet (but most bags don't anyway). the color is more like a dark lime green or a lighter olive green (see photo for color comparison and a side-by-side view of the other case i bought). another reviewer called this a "pea green" and that is pretty accurate. i like the color a lot actually. i really wanted this case to work so i could have a smaller thinner one that i could hide under my car seat. this is the second time i have purchased a 15" built case and have it not fit the 15.4" macbook pro. i learned my lesson. on the built site, it lists two categories: 15" and 15.4". i should have paid attention better, however this color is discontinued so it is not clear what category it fell into. i took the benefit of the doubt but was wrong. this page is a little misleading because it lists the case a fitting 13-15" laptops but does not list any dimensions. make sure if you ever buy a built case for a 15.4" computer that you get a 15.4" case or verify the dimensions are larger than your laptop width.
summary: great bag but again, doesn't really fit the 15.4" macbook pro

reviewText: i tried a variety of different cases of this general style.  i liked this one because the magnets are strong enough to actually hold the lid shut securely.  the lid won't flop open like the ayl case of this style.  the problem i experienced was that after about 2 months the leather edges at joints/bend-points started coming apart.  there's some sort of material the manufacturer uses around the edge to fuse the inner and outer leather pieces.  this came off at the joints.  it was still functional, it just looked ugly.  also, the border leather around the bevel didn't lay flat against the screen--it kind of bowed out.  again, didn't hurt the functionality, just looked a little sloppy. finally, and this isn't an indictment of this case in particular, but i found this style case--the angles aren't really suited to my viewing habits.  your choices are either near perpendicular (80 degrees) or somewhat flat (~20 degrees). neither of those worked all that well for me.  instead i bought an ayl case that can do a 40 and 60 degree angle, that despite being bulkier than this style, works better for me.  ymmv on that point.
summary: nice, but started falling about after <3 months

reviewText:
if you are just looking for basic functions and simply expect the router to work without the hassle. this one would work and it seems stable, although it is sold with a pre-release fw and you may need to upgrade it to the 1st release fw which doesn't seem to have changed anything.
however, for this price you'd expect to be able to use the other features as well which seems to not work at all. few of the issues:
1. gigabit - only the wan has a setup but when set on 1000m it won't work at all, so it syncs on 100bt only
2. after changing the gigabit back to auto, it took about 4 reboots before it was able to acquire an ip from my cable modem
3. static routing - does not work
3. updating/saving/rebooting take forever
4. not least in importance - there is no one to talk to in the us for support. they have a number but i don't think they've actually manned that function. so you get an answering machine and when you are ready to leave a messages, the machine announces it's too full and there is no way to leave one. email? no one answered.
5. throughput is not that great in very close proximity to the router

bottom line. it is an expensive modem for what it provides. i wouldn't recommend it.
summary: throughput is not that great in very close proximity to the router bottom line

reviewText:
i wanted to love this lens. sadly, it simply doesn't perform well.

the focus issues with this lens have been written about ad nauseum, but i found that the focus issues manifested themselves differently than what i'd read here. it's not that the lens doesn't focus - it's that it focuses on the wrong thing.

i was shooting this lens on a d40, which has five-point autofocus. i shot a series of engagement pictures entirely with this lens, and i used this lens heavily for a wedding. the amount of light that you get with an f/1.4 is incredible, and was a lifesaver in a dimly-lit church, but i lost dozens and dozens of shots because they were slightly out of focus. the lens would claim to be focused on one point, but would have focused ever so slightly on something just out of the bracket. the result is hard to tell on camera during the shoot, but unmistakable when viewing the pictures full-size.

furthermore, this lens has no manual focus override. you can't grab the focus ring, and there's no switch. the only thing you can do is use the af lock on your camera.

if all you are doing is still portrait work in which you have careful and controlled handling of your subject, this lens is superb. portraits are beautiful with it, and i found the bokeh to be very pleasing. the shots that *were* in focus are colorful, well-lit, superb pictures.

ultimately, though, this lens isn't versatile enough due to the focusing issues. it's too bad - sigma nearly hit a home run with this one.

if you're considering this lens and have read all the reviews as i did, please hear me on this: the focusing issues *are* a problem, and they *will* cause you to lose pictures. it's not a matter of, as i thought, some people not knowing how to use the lens. the lens has focusing issues, plain and simple.

i guess i'll try the new nikon 50mm f/1.4, although i sure wish it was the wider 30mm of this lens. so close, but so far.

reviewText: if you examine the range of usb microphones for sale at amazon, you will find lower end ones in the $25 range that are good for the times when you simply want to have a microphone and quality isn't much of an issue. such microphones lack sensitivity and range, and give mediocre sound quality at best. this samson microphone is not a high end microphone, but will give you good sound quality at a lower end price point. its cardioid design has a heart shaped pickup pattern, meaning it works best with sounds coming from one side of it, and covering to a lesser extent those sounds coming from the surrounding area on the same side. so if you use it for vocals or with an instrument, it will be more sensitive to the side with the vocalist or the instrument, less sensitive to the audience side, but still pick up the band albeit at a much lower background level. this mic is more sensitive than a typical cheap "rock band" grade mic, so it works best when you are about a foot away unless you use a screen (not included). it will pick up sounds from eight feet away, but they will sound like they are eight feet away. in other words, it works as a personal mic, and if you want something to record multiple people or instruments, you'd want one of these for each person or instrument. if you are looking for something with a choice of patterns such as cardioid, stereo, bidirectional and omnidirectional, and want something potentially sensitive enough to pick up a sound clearly from 10 feet away as if it were at the microphone, you could expect to pay at least double for something like a blue microphones yeti usb microphone. if you want to pay less, there are a variety of options but don't expect the sound quality to be up to this one. if you are looking for a good mono recording mic, with a cardioid pattern (probably the best pattern for practical purposes) then you get a lot of quality for the price range. for a home user who wants enough quality for something to sound good but who isn't ready to go all out and spend lots more money, this mic is a good choice. likewise, if you need to buy several without breaking the bank, this will also fit the bill. it will work as a plug and play microphone with compatible systems, but you can download software from the manufacturer to get a lot more control over it.

reviewText:
first impression: huge pop in speakers and headphones whenever you turn power on or off. who designs this?  one has to disconnect speakers every time before turning this thing on and off?  and turn it on and off you will have to do frequently, as scarlett 18i8 disconnects from all digital outputs very frequently. but before we get to this, does it really have 18i8 (18 inputs, 8 outputs)?  that is the magic of counting.

on the front: four balanced xlr microphone combo inputs, either of which can also act as a balanced line input should you use a 1/4" jack. switching between mic/line goes automatically based on which plug you are using.  phantom powered in pairs (1+2), (3+4). either of inputs 1,2 can be switched (but via software only) to high-z.  you can use usb as input, too (but see what happens with that later).

on the back: four balanced line inputs, one stereo spdif input (rca jack), one midi input (5-pin din) and an adat that can be used to connect another device that has an adat output.  short of such device, we are counting eight balanced inputs (out of which four have preamps), one stereo spdif and one midi.  that is somewhere between 8 and 11, and nowhere close to 18.  you could argue that midi can be daisy-chained in which case the total can be as much as midi permits.  too bad focusrite did not catch on that idea.

outputs: two stereo headphone outputs, two mono monitor outputs, one stereo spdif (rca jack), one midi (5 pin din).  this makes five outputs unless you are going to split the headphone output into two channels and plug it elsewhere. other than spdif which only carries two channels, to capture multiple channels digitally you have to use usb.

levels, routing and digital capture can be set only via focusrite mixcontrol software which means it needs a computer connection via usb.  as it is clear from the above, everything digital hinges on that usb connection. the only other output usable for digital recording is spdif (two channels only).

well, does the usb work?  not for long.  the moment any of your channel inputs clips (touches the 0 db mark), you enter a roulette which usually, but not always, results in scarlett 18i8 disappearing from windows.  at that point, digital capture stops and mixcontrol shows "hardware not connected".

what of there is no clipping?  turns out, it still can disconnect.  not as often, but it will.  mixcontrol will show the connection but there will be no signal coming.  again, useless.

new drivers/firmware etc?  minor changes but the behaviour stays essentially the same - disconnect after disconnect.

what about mixcontrol?  it may be the culprit, as with mixcontrol turned off, the 18i8 disconnects less often.  however, you cannot have 18i8 running stable and connected to a pc with mixcontrol active.  you could close mixcontrol, but then you lose the ability to re-route, mute channels, change levels etc.  there are no usable physical controls other than four preamp knobs, monitor and headphone level knobs and phantom power switches. without mixcontrol the device cannot be controlled and with mixcontrol the device is unstable.

verdict - do not buy.

purchased 2011-12??  worse electronic device i've ever had!!
remote buttons were so soft, if you reach for it in semi-dark and just graze a button by accident . . .  then the button activates and whatever you're watching disappears, with the new function  . .
and what's the biggest button on the remote??

netflix!!

and there's no way to navigate back to the movie you just shut-off, so you usually shut off the player & start over from scratch.
and that damned remote bounce's off walls & activates netflix thru couch cushions.

remote aside, the player itself also sucked!
it was very slow & finicky to read/recognize a disc, be it blu-ray, dvd or otherwise.
sometimes if you stopped in middle of movie it would remember where you stopped & offer a "resume?" function.
often, just as you were ready to start a movie, it would blank out or request a firmware/software update.
i could never get it to update via wi fi, so it was upstairs to the desktop, with a thumb drive, another 20 minutes wasted.

i actually had to hook up my 12 y/old panasonic dvd player beneath it to play movies when the samsung was too finicky to even realize there was a disc in it.  got a 3-way optical selector so i didn't have to swap plugs when my back-up dvd player came in to save the day.

finally, last month it started getting "grabby" with discs: not ejecting them.
door wouldn't open & either front-console or remote eject button wouldn't cough up the disc.
i finally took a screwdriver & pliers to the eject door, ripped it off & the tray out, being careful not to scratch the library dvd, since that was worth more than the samsung bd-e5900 player . . .

and, thusly, committed myself to get a real blu ray player, a sony.
paid $89 for the new sony & works fantastic!!
paid $220 for this samsung, was the worse electronic / entertainment equipment i've ever brought home!

the unit didn't show up. i checked the tracking number and the delivery time was 8 days - 6 business days from the order date!

i wrote to oppo and got again a snarky reply. to the effect that i'd just have to wait.

i called fedex and told them that if the package should show up i would refuse it (who would want an electronic device that had, suppossedly been on a truck for 9 days in 100 degree heat.)

i wrote to oppo about the fact that i would be refusing the package that still had no delivery date and asked for my credit card to be credited.

from oppo i got a terse response that when fedex returned the unit to them intact they would credit me only the price of the unit and i would have to eat the cost of shipping!!

the assumption is that if the package is completely lost then i have to pay for the whole thing! they assume no responsibility.

if their customer service is this sarcastic and brutally nasty when i have paid for and not even received the unit i shudder to think what they would be like if there were a problem with the unit themselves.

i bought a sony ns-75h. i'm very happy with it.

reviewText:
pros:
-affordable
-compact
-nice smart auto feature

cons:
-video quality very sub-par for the price
-"cmos sensor" with nothing near cmos quality
-snapshot feature at 1.6m hardly worth using

i will admit, with all of the hype this camcorder is getting i feel i must throw my 2 cents in as well. in using this camcorder solely for the purpose of youtube video production, i will be the first to admit the so-claimed video quality is very poor, especially if you plan to watch the recorded videos on something other than the video cameras screen. videos looked great on the built in lcd, but when blown up on a computer and watched fullscreen on a 1080p monitor the quality is not as promising as i was hoping, especially for a camera with a recommended starting price as $200. i can't say i expect much from a $200 video camera, but my 720p webcam that i bought for $100 roughly 6 years ago records better video than this camera. being nobody new to dslr cameras and video cameras, i will admit that while i seem a little harsh in my critical review of the video quality of a $200 camcorder, i'm still not ashamed to admit that comparatively speaking, my old webcam takes better videos.
summary: video quality not as good as everyone makes it seem
