i bought this box back in may and have been a defacto beta tester ever since.  this is an inexpensive box that acts as a hdtv tuner and a recorder.  it has hdmi as well as rf coax, component and composite video.  i purchased it mainly because i've been looking for an inexpensive digital tv recorder for ota tv that i could recommend to people who want to "cut the cord."  this box is a step in the right direction, but it needs a fair amount of work.  the components are cheap, including the tuner, and that causes some problems.  the current issue remote is small and difficult to use, but iview is in the process of replacing it.  there is a new official firmware release that fixes a lot of the problems with the box.  it's also possible to run the firmware for the homeworx hw-150pvr on it if you have a homeworx remote or a logitech harmony remote (remote codes for the two boxes are different, but the interior hardware is for the most part the same).

the good is that it has great picture quality and it records in the same quality as what is broadcast.  i'm recording to a toshiba canvio 1tb drive, and as far as i know haven't had any drive related problems though there is some question whether the power supply in the iview 3500stb will support a usb powered hard drive long term.  the hard drive can be plugged into a computer and the files can be viewed on the computer, or transfered to the computer.  i've also been able to watch the recordings using the playon mymedia channel on my roku, so for you roku folks out there, there is that option (video hangs if you try to skip commercials though).

the bad is that, at least with past firmware, the box has problems recording some channels which the tuner has difficulty tuning.  i've also had a problem with the tuner stopping working and the box needing to be unplugged to fix it.  i believe that most of the other problems (midnight and daily and weekly recording bugs) have been fixed with the new firmware.

overall this box shows the potential for inexpensive over the air and clear qam (clear qam isn't long for this world since the fcc has authorized the encryption of all cable channels including basic broadcast channels) digital video recorders.  the basic concept is sound, and with firmware updates this will be a decent box.  if the hardware was updated (better tuner and higher output power supply) this would be a serious cable cord cutting device.

my first boom type reflector holder i bought on amazon was the only one where the pole actually fit correctly in the clamping disks. it is truly a shame that this one seems to be unavailable for an indeterminate amount of time. (nulink)

so i bought this one for twice the price from cowboy studio and the results were not acceptable. at first i did not understand the reviews, thinking it was identical to the one i got from nulink but now i get it.

the hub or clamping disc has 4 size holes running laterally though it. it is ingenious actually, look at a hole it is one size, rotate 90 and the hole is still there but it is smaller, or larger. in this way poles of 4 distinct sizes can be accommodated in the pivot mechanism. i thought people just weren't understanding how to use the thing. well, i finally got mine and the boom pole is too big for the smallest size hole and too small for the next size up. its quite annoying. it would have been so easy for the manufacturer to make sure the pole was the proper diameter, or the clamp fit correctly. but they didn't bother apparently. so quite useful becomes worthless all for a couple of millimeters.

if you force it to fit and tighten the clamp, it will warp and eventually lose its ability to hold at all. so all in all, this thing is quite the waste of time and money.
summary: it would be so easy to get it right. it is a shame they didnt.

i have no idea how a) the manufacturer can claim 500mbps performance, an b) the high user ratings.

reviewText: i purchased this, assuming that if it was marketed for travelers, and thus it would work overseas.  in the future, i'll have to always check tech specs before buying.  it works great in the us (110v).  it's compact, has five outlets that allow for transformers, and packs in luggage well.  however, it does not work with other overseas voltages (220v).  in the past, i've always traveled overseas with 1 or 2 universal travel adapters, and a us power strip so that i can plug in my computer, cell phone, pda, camera, video camera, etc. all at the same time.  this works well, as many power strips don't have any electronics in them.  they simply transfer the power from wall to the outlets.  of course, power strips are more bulky than this item, and one must ensure all electronics plugged into it are 220v compatible.  i didn't notice the "reset" button on this device until i tried to use it overseas and blew the breaker in my room.  this is so that if you overload it, you can unplug something and then simply reset it, rather than having to buy a fuse.  it also caused the fuse to blow in the kensington universal adapter that i plugged it into.  this is a good item for travel in the us, but don't plan on using it overseas.

reviewText:
for $10 its a decent case, its not the super hard plastic i was expecting, but it is made of rigid rubber-like plastic. i think it will likely protect your phone from minor falls, but don't expect too much from it if you drop your phone on naked concrete or in a rocky area. the lip of the case is about 1mm high, which will protect it if you drop it on a perfectly flat surface, but if there are pebbles or any jagged edges in the ground, your screen will be doomed to shattering.

it is frosted, but if you have the standard silver version of the one, then you will be pleasantly surprised that the frosting does not really show up at all when you install the case. you can see the shiny metal glory of the one perfectly through the case as if it was perfectly clear. with that frosting though, it will be harder to notice any scratches or dings on the case, which is a nice thing.

the only thing i have to complain about, is that the case tends to make pressing the volume buttons much harder than it should be. if you don't have nails, or if you have long nails, it may take quite a bit of extra effort to press the volume buttons. they decided to have a bit of a cutout on the inside of the case for the volume buttons, but i think it would have worked perfectly well if they just had the buttons flush against the rest of the inside of the case. now that extra .5mm of distance you need to push the buttons on the case really make a difference. i may decide to slightly modify the case with glue or tape or something in the future to fix the volume button issue.

it fulfills all that i expected of it, short of the annoyance of the volume button design on the case, i would recommend it as a minimal bulk-adding case for the htc one that allows you to marvel at the beautiful construction of the device.

edit (10/10/13): i fixed the mushy volume buttons. my recommendation for a fix that is simple and easy: get a post-it note, then cut strips of the sticky part of the note that are the size of the hollow in the case of the volume buttons, stack them, then put it sticky side to the case on the inside, against the hollow, filling it. i tried 5 layers, and it is pretty much perfect now. the button is easy to push, but if you just slide your finger along the side, you won't accidentally push the button.

i received this item to review based on my interest in photography.  i must say that initially i was skeptical i would like this item.  but, after some use, i must report this item is quite nice, roomy and useful.

1. what's in the box?: you receive this bag.  the bag is a interesting purple/mauve color with an attached strap for the shoulder.

2.  aesthetic?: the bag is a fairly good size.  it is not as large as is implied by the pictures.  also, the bag is a interesting purple mauve color.  the color is interesting because it is not something i would automatically select of i had another choice.  the color is not unattractive, but it is not exactly the most masculine color available. the straps are an off-white color.  the material is a nice, quality appearing rip-stop nylon that seems pretty sturdy. although the color is not great, the bag is pleasingly designed.

3. use:?  this item was used with a dslr, with an additional lens, ipad tablet, and other camera accessories.  on of the first things noticed with this bag is the zippered areas.  there are two pockets on the side of the item which can store a fair amount of stuff.  on the interior, which is made very accessible with the twin zipper system. the interior has a included velcro 'box' which also has a pull-over zip-tie rig that allows some water protection for the item of that is desired.  nice feature.  there is also a zippered pocket which can be used for camera cards, lens caps or any number of items.  it is also mesh.

the 'box' includes a replaceable padding which can be used as a partition in the box, or as a extra bit of padding on the bottom.  the bag is not especially padded by the way, so this is not a bag for ultimate protection.  although the bag is not huge, i have found that it does accommodate a good amount of stuff including a dslr.  it is not the bag for you if you need to carry more than a dslr, a 150mm lens (or equivalent) and some other things.  the bag also allows the user to put a water bottle in a special strapped pocket.  this is a nice touch!

4. observations:

 after using the bag, i like it quite a bit.  the shoulder strap allows the user to use this as a sling.  i like this feature quite a bit as it allows the user to grab the camera pretty easily.  the bag is pretty roomy for most uses.  i have used it hiking and the shoulder strap was not especially noticeable during the hike.  this was appreciated.

a few things bother me about this item.  the color as i mentioned is not the greatest (one good point is you will see it easily!).  secondly, the lack of more padding on the bottom means don't rely on this item to be the sole protection for your camera.  also, the current price is not cheap.  i must be honest, at the price point of 70ish dollars, i am not sure i would run and grab this item.  yes, it is nice, but it is also expensive.  for a short hike with your camera to take pictures, this could be very useful, however. for use as say as a carry-on at the airport to contain your personal items, camera and a tablet, this would work as well.

overall, this is a nice item.  give the above, i would certainly consider the item if i wanted a nice sling type bag,  the cost is a consideration, however.
summary: for what it is, quite a nice item.

2.  aesthetic?: the bag is a fairly good size.  it is not as large as is implied by the pictures.  also, the bag is a interesting purple mauve color.  the color is interesting because it is not something i would automatically select of i had another choice.  the color is not unattractive, but it is not exactly the most masculine color available. the straps are an off-white color.  the material is a nice, quality appearing rip-stop nylon that seems pretty sturdy. although the color is not great, the bag is pleasingly designed.

3. use:?  this item was used with a dslr, with an additional lens, ipad tablet, and other camera accessories.  on of the first things noticed with this bag is the zippered areas.  there are two pockets on the side of the item which can store a fair amount of stuff.  on the interior, which is made very accessible with the twin zipper system. the interior has a included velcro 'box' which also has a pull-over zip-tie rig that allows some water protection for the item of that is desired.  nice feature.  there is also a zippered pocket which can be used for camera cards, lens caps or any number of items.  it is also mesh.

the 'box' includes a replaceable padding which can be used as a partition in the box, or as a extra bit of padding on the bottom.  the bag is not especially padded by the way, so this is not a bag for ultimate protection.  although the bag is not huge, i have found that it does accommodate a good amount of stuff including a dslr.  it is not the bag for you if you need to carry more than a dslr, a 150mm lens (or equivalent) and some other things.  the bag also allows the user to put a water bottle in a special strapped pocket.  this is a nice touch!

4. observations:

 after using the bag, i like it quite a bit.  the shoulder strap allows the user to use this as a sling.  i like this feature quite a bit as it allows the user to grab the camera pretty easily.  the bag is pretty roomy for most uses.  i have used it hiking and the shoulder strap was not especially noticeable during the hike.  this was appreciated.

a few things bother me about this item.  the color as i mentioned is not the greatest (one good point is you will see it easily!).  secondly, the lack of more padding on the bottom means don't rely on this item to be the sole protection for your camera.  also, the current price is not cheap.  i must be honest, at the price point of 70ish dollars, i am not sure i would run and grab this item.  yes, it is nice, but it is also expensive.  for a short hike with your camera to take pictures, this could be very useful, however. for use as say as a carry-on at the airport to contain your personal items, camera and a tablet, this would work as well.

overall, this is a nice item.  give the above, i would certainly consider the item if i wanted a nice sling type bag,  the cost is a consideration, however. for what it is, quite a nice item.

reviewText:
i've been using the microsoft wireless lazer desktop 6000 for about a month now, but i will be returning it.  i really don't know exactly what is causing the problems i am having with it, but life is too short to troubleshoot when logitech makes a product that seems to work better.

i have had problems with both keyboard and mouse.

previously i was having more problems with my keyboard, but it seems to be working slightly better now.  for a period of time, it wasn't recording every keystroke, which is a bit of a problem in a keyboard.  the wireless aspect seems to be working better now, though i do still get too-frequent notices that the signal is weak.  the keys do seem to require a pretty solid strike, even when the wireless if functioning.  the upside is that my fingers are in better muscular conditioning now than they've been in for years.  the shift key also seems to give me caps well into the third and fourth letter sometimes, and i can hardly attribute that to any superman typing ability.

the mouse has issues that don't seem to be going away.  the overall feel of the mouse is a bit to plastic-y and slick for me, but i would have been able to get over that if the functionality was ok.  sadly, the functionality is pretty terrible in my experience.  the left click -- perhaps the most key part of the mouse -- is very tempermental.  sometimes left click works appropriately; sometimes it requires a second or third angry attempt to get it to do anything.  as for the laser tracker, it doesn't seem to work well at all.  sometimes i am unable to register forward/backward motion and sometimes i can't get it to register sideways.  raising it to a slightly angle seems to help, but that shouldn't be necessary.  i do use the mouse on a slick surface, but it is polished wood not glass.  again, the issue could be related to the wireless signal.

i readily admit that i could have interference in my office.  i have the receiver about 1-2 feet from both keyboard and mouse (which should be close enough), but i do have 3 flatscreens and the cpu in close proximity.  i also have shielded flourescent lighting.  but that is my environment, and the part of my enviroment that is going to change isn't the lighting or monitors, it's the keyboard and mouse.

i'm hoping the logitech proves superior.

reviewText:
i like the design and features of the garmin i5, but i simply cannot give it more than three stars for two reasons:

1) it takes too long to locate satellites
2) it often loses the signal

granted, i live in a wooded area, but i have been using the i5 for two months now and it loses the satellite signal here in the southeast on cloudy and/or rainy days quite often. perhaps this is the unit i own, or the slope of the windshield in my ford explorer. when i have used this unit in california and texas in various rentals vehicles, the problems seemed much less prevalent. the manual clearly explains that the signal may be weak or lost when in the shadow of large building or in heavy wooded areas. however, my unit seems to briefly lose the signal anytime we have heavy cloud cover - repeatedly, which causes the unit to inform me that it has lost the signal - repeatedly. that can be irritating when it happens 10 times in 10 minutes.

the unit itself has a bright, crisp display that might be too small for seniors to see very easily. it's right for me. the navigation is good, and i have used the unit to find a number of locations that would have taken much longer to get to without it. it has also failed to find a number of locations in recently constructed neighborhoods.

when the i5 works, it makes me happy. but when it frequently loses the signal at an inconvenient time, i wish i had purchased a product with better reception.

reviewText: here's the short story on this camera. it should be a five-star camera. the photo quality is great. the speed is wonderful. the handling and ergonomics are fantastic. the twisting lcd and the viewfinder are sharp, large, and bright. the slow motion is really fun. unfortunately, the thing that really separates this camera from the crowd, the manual twist zoom lens, is a near failure. i'm really scratching my head as to why what is perhaps the biggest selling point of this model is poorly done. it's not remotely smooth. it drags and takes so much oomph to turn that the camera moves in your gripped hand. when you get near the telephoto end you can actually hear (and feel) what could be clicking. again, in all other respects, this is easily a five-star camera in this price range. i'm stumped why such a big feature as the manual zoom is bad. read other reviews about this problem and believe them. i wanted to like this camera, but the manual zoom feels almost like a defect. others have commented that they've returned their units thinking it actually was defective, but the replacements performed the same way.

i wanted a lens over 200mm for my arsenal and unfortunately, if you stick with the nikon brand, there aren't too many options. i chose the 80-400, but i have to say that it's the one nikon lens purchase i've had the most trouble getting excited over. not that it isn't a great product - it is - it's just that it seemed like a step back in time since this lens hasn't kept up with the features of nikon's phenomenally good pro lenses throughout the rest of the product line. in the end, i felt like the choice was to "settle" for this product, or spend several times more money on (say) the excellent 200-400 zoom instead. or, i suppose you could wait for the next upgrade, but i've already been waiting a few years with no result.

the lens itself is large and heavy, somewhat "thicker" than say, a 70-200 2.8 - but not by a huge amount. it feels balanced on any of nikon's larger cameras, but it is quite a handful. unlike some, i find the tripod collar adequate, although i understand many recommend the kirk collar as an important upgrade. honestly, i tend to hand-hold the lens more often than not, so i usually have the tripod collar removed altogether. i find it's large enough to get in the way of where i'd naturally want to put my hands. the other comment on construction quality is that it really looks like a "legacy" product. not being an afs focusing system, it sports that old "m/a" focus control, and it also still has a manual aperture selector. which isn't to say that it's not a high quality lens - it is, it's just showing its age. otherwise, the controls operate smoothly and it does feel to be built to last.

from an optical point of view, i found the lens to perform better than i expected. at both extremes (80 and 400), i notice photos are a little soft in the corners with the lens wide open, but if you use f/8 or smaller, results are uniformly sharp corner to corner (this is only really noticeable on an fx sensor...dx cameras are very good even wide open). contrast and color are also good, and images generally have that "pop" you get from any top quality lens. i have the latest 70-200 2.8 lens, and at 200mm, i'd say that  images from the 80-400 are nearly - but not quite - as good overall. the 80-400 is slightly less contrasty, making some shots appear a little "flat", and the 80-400 also seems slightly more prone to flare when pointed in the direction of a bright light source.

i find the vr system works well, and with the lens zoomed out to 400mm, i can usually get sharp results with shutter speeds in the vicinity of 1/100 second, maybe a little less.

as everyone else points out, the autofocus system is somewhat slow and noisy if you're used to afs lenses. at longer focal lengths in darker spots, it also tends to hunt. i've learned to simply switch off the autofocus and use the manual controls in these situations.

overall, i guess i'm happy with this lens, but this is one of those lenses that i'll be looking to upgrade as soon as nikon comes out with an afs version that's hopefully about a stop faster and not triple the price.
summary: great lens, but starting to feel a little dated

reviewText:
i sometimes need to use my ipad 2 as a laptop, and i find it difficult to do heavy typing, etc., on the touchscreen keyboard. i only use my ipad for this purpose about 25% of the time, so i didn't need one of the budget-busting $150+ bluetooth keyboard cases, since those are better suited to "road warriors" who normally use their ipads as laptop replacements.  this ihome keyboard case seemed to meet my dual need for a protective case with an integrated bluetooth keyboard, at a reasonable price point.

unfortunately, however, this turned out to be another case of "you get what you pay for."  first off, although this is supposed to be a "slim" keyboard case, it's actually quite bulky.  and the magnets that hold the front flap of the case closed are pretty weak (and lose even more strength over time), so it's too easy for the front cover of the case to flop open.  not only does that expose your ipad screen to the elements, but it also exposes the keyboard of the case, risking mistaken key-presses and broken keys.  additionally, although it is very difficult to get your ipad to snap securely into this case, it is exceedingly easy for the ipad to fall out of the case, especially when the case is in "laptop mode."

this leads me to the main failing of this ihome keyboard case: it cannot be used on your lap.  when it's in laptop-mode, it must be sitting on a completely flat, level surface, otherwise it's virtually useless.  on your lap (a naturally uneven surface), even the slightest movement will cause the ipad to slide out through the open edge of the case and onto the floor.  even on a desk or tray-table, one wrong move, and the folded "triangle" that props the ipad up, will fall flat on its back.  if you'll be using this keyboard case in laptop-mode for several hours, plan on spending a lot of that time refolding the back of the case into the "triangle" and re-propping-up your ipad.  quite frustrating, to the say the least.  finally, the ipad often stops responding to certain keys pressed on the bluetooth keyboard, for no apparent reason.  the first time this happened, i was halfway though typing an email when i noticed that the text on screen was littered with typos caused by omitted letters (key-presses that weren't detected by the ipad).  re-pairing the bluetooth keyboard with your ipad usually helps, but it's pretty irritating to have to stop right in the middle of typing to fix this keyboard issue.

all in all, it seems like it's impossible to get a good quality ipad bluetooth keyboard case for less than $100.  i paid about half that much for this ihome case, but it wasn't worth the annoyance and un-user-friendliness.  save yourself the aggravation and pony-up the extra money for a proper and usable bluetooth keyboard case.

grade: d-

this is just a plain sweetheart of a lens.  it covers the useful 18-35 mm range (which is 27-52mm on a nikon digital slr, which is a very useful range).  this lens costs less than half the price of the (expensive) professional nikon 17-35, and does almost as nice a job. sufficiently nice, in fact, that most amateurs will not discern much, if any, difference.  while not built like a tank, i think that the quality of construction on this one is excellent, and more than adequate for enthusiastic amateurs and even some pros.

on a nikon digital slr, which will use the center portion of this lens (due to the size of the sensor in the slr) you can expect excellent, even spectacular results.  this is a fabulous lens for landscape and nature shots, portraits, or just plain walking around taking pictures.  someone who only wanted one lens that was not a telephoto could do much worse than to select this excellent, versatile lens.  this one is great for parties, vacations, and the works.

the images i have shot with this lens have all featured superb contrast, are very sharp, and have beautiful color rendition.  there just is not a lot not to like about this lens. i give it 4 stars for overall performance, but 5 stars for value and price/performance.  some lenses just get it all together and work and become keepers.  this is one of those.
summary: a sweetheart!  a versatile performer, solid and fun to use!

reviewText:
first off, i purchased this processor from a local retailer, as the price was slightly cheaper and at the time, i needed it right away.  but, i figured i'd review it on amazon, as this is my usual stop for computer hardware purchases.

(+):  6/12 (cores/threads), 40 lanes of pcie 3.0, supports 4 video cards, huge improvement of multi-thread performance, 4-channel ddr4 support, 15mb cache, decent overclocks with standard cooling; even better with water or aio units.  if you had a 5930k, this could be a suitable upgrade depending on your scenario.

all in all, this processor is insanely quick, especially in multi-threaded/core applications.  in terms of raw power, you're only going to be bested by the 6900k & 6950x, but not by much.  if you're looking for top performance and need several ssds, m.2 storage and sli video cards, this is the processor you're going to want.  outside of that, you're not going to even come close to needing this amount of power 'under the hood'.

(-):  it's hard to list cons, but the price and marketing ploy of 35% improvement over haswell-e drop this 1-star.  is it that big of an improvement?  in real world tests, no.  in synthetic benchmarks, you'll see a difference in scores, but not in true performance.  possibly, you'd see a larger gap if you were max'ing out your 5930k with nearly every lane and doing extensive cpu tasks; but even today you'll never see a use case for that.  additionally, intel charges you a premium to be in this realm, much like they did for the haswell-e processors.  is it worth the cost for 99% of consumers....no!

all in all, this is a great processor that outperforms most on the market.  in terms of gaming, don't buy this processor.  it's overkill and truly a waste of extra money that can be used for a better gpu or monitor setup.  most game benchmarks actually favor the i7-6700k and i5-6600k for the higher clock speeds you're able to get on those chips.  if you're just looking for a total gaming workhorse, the 6700k checks and exceeds all your boxes.

if you can wait out a little bit, i'd recommend waiting for a stepping or two to come out, then purchase.  some people on computer hardware forums have mentioned they didn't get a good overclocking chip from the 'silicon lottery'.

reviewText:
if you've tried many headphones in this price range you already know a lot of them are too small in diameter, or have too shallow of earcups, to really sit over the ears. many end up at least partly sitting *on* the ear which makes them a lot less comfortable and also means the ear pads don't seal as well letting more outside ambient noise in (and more music out). there are a few with big enough earcups in this price range but they usually sound pretty awrful and/or clamp your head like a vice and/or have really bad build quality. i'm happy to say the koss ur-20 suffers from none of these problems.

pluses: they fit very comfortably over the ear, they're lightweight, the have a straight cord that won't tug at the headphones like a coiled cord, they have just enough tension in the headband to keep them in place while still being really comfortable, they have decent isolation.

the sound: they're reasonably sensitive and will play fairly loud with most portable players. you don't need anything fancy or a headphone amp. they have decent fairly accurate bass response. they don't rattle or obviously distort with heavier bass at higher volumes like many cheap headphones. the bad news is the midrange is a little "nasal" and the highs are a little edgy. but, at this price range, you can't expect perfection.

comparison: as a comparison, the hundred dollar sennheiser hd-280 pro doesn't sound much better, has earcups too small to properly ft around bigger ears, has an annoying coiled cord, and clamps the head with way too much force. the sennheiser hd-201 is much closer in price to the ur-20 but has earcups that are way too shallow, less isolation, and inferior deep bass performance but otherwise similar sound.

negatives: the main reason for knocking a star off was the midrange and highs as mentioned above. they're also kinda big and a little "clunky" (but not heavy). they adjustment for the earcups on the headband is also prone to slipping when they're not being worn. they don't fold so they're not so good for shoving in a backpack. the isolation is decent but not as good as heavier, tighter clamps, pro cans made for studio work.
summary: genuine over the ear sealed back inexpensive headphones with decent sound

reviewText:
my old speedstream recently choked and died hence i was on the market for a new wireless router.  i wanted 802.11g/b, vpn passthrough to get to my corporate network, cheap, and most importantly - painless.

my first attempt was the d-link di-624m.  that product did not meet these requirements.  i suffered lots of pain, going through 3 before i managed to update the firmware on one without it being permanently killed in the process.  also, i spent hours fighting to get my vpn working.  d-link tech support failed to make it work.  i eventually figured it out myself but only after more painful hours spent.  also, the d-link must be non-compliant/buggy with some standard used to detect changes in network configuration and automatically fix up the links.  i had to make sure my cable modem was always turned on after the router or it often wouldn't ever get properly connected.

anyway, the d-link sucked.

so i picked up this linksys wrt54g (version 4) and had absolutely zero issues. vpn worked right out of the box.  interaction with my motorola cable modem is seamless and automatic.  i just plugged the thing in and it all worked perfectly.  that was what i have been looking for - painless.  the linksys also has many more advanced features.  i've not used these yet but the menues are full of lots of options.  the only feature i couldn't find (that the d-link has) is the ability to force static allocation of private ip addresses based on mac address.

thank you linksys for a solid product that saves us busy people time and frustration!

reviewText:
zune's os is really a version of windows ce and the user interface reminds me of media center a little bit, which is ok, but the news of a possible linux version for the zune is something to look forward to.

pros:
-cheaper
cheaper than a 5.5 ipod.  it's perfect for someone who simply wants to hold a whole lot of mp3's without worrying too much about looks or paying too much.  amazon's price is a great bargain.
-fm tuner
i still listen to my local stations, and the best part is that the song title and artist shows up, so i can find out the name of a new song download it later on.
-wallpaper/pictures
the zune software organizes the files into folders exactly as i have it in my documents.  much easier to find and replace the wallpapers.
-playlist
easier to stay organized and create customized lists than an 5.5 ipod, even when not connected to the computer.
-sound
definitely louder than video ipods.  at least for me.
-battery charging
surprisingly quick the first time around.  didn't take the three hours i thought it would.
-file formats
does convert mp4 into wmv automatically for videos.

cons:
-buttons
not a true click wheel as in an ipod.  nothing is marked except play/pause and back buttons.  takes a little getting used to.
-software installation
several installation problems including multiple zunes showing up under device manager, not detecting the zune the first time, and not being able to delete empty playlists from the device.  the software was probably the most frustrating part of the experience.  but it uses less memory when running on my computer than itunes, and i didn't have any problems upgrading the firmware once i got it working.
-headphones
the packaged ones are uncomfortable and sound terrible.  bought a pair of koss instead.

haven't tried the a/v out or wireless sharing features yet.

has potential to be a strong standalone mp3 player, for the price, without the need for all the bells and whistles like xbox connectivity or wireless sharing.  but it would be great to have apps like an ebook reader or internet browser for use with wifi networks.

reviewText:
the s3 is an interesting stereo speaker meant to be used as part of a whole-house system, similar to what sonos offers. unfortunately, it seems to be fairly uk-oriented for now, and does not yet support major offerings needed on the us market, such as siriusxm.
the pureconnect app (free for ios and android) can control all the various pure speakers in your house; they can be paired very cleverly so that one speaker plays the left channel and another the right (similar to what sonos play:3 and play:5 speakers can do). unlike sonos, the system connects directly to your wifi network and does not require a bridge.

despite its wifi connection and ios ties, the pure system does not support airplay, a very unfortunate omission -- although it's always possible that pure will offer it in a future update.

audio quality is excellent; the rub is that you are limited to playing what the pure app gives you access to, unless you use bluetooth streaming (which limits you to staying within a few feet of the speaker) or the audio in jack (which requires tethering your audio device to the speaker). airplay would have let you steer audio from almost any music or video player directly to the pure speaker with better quality and reliability than bluetooth.

the pureconnect app is pretty, but not very intuitive and nags infuriatingly, requesting that you sign up for its free service. streaming choices are limited.

the jongo and pure system has a lot of potential, but as it stands in september 2013, i find it difficult to recommend: there are many bluetooth speakers that are just as competent, and its wifi features are just not mature enough to be worth the price in my opinion. the software still has a long way to go before pure can be considered a serious sonos competitor, but the hardware can definitely support it. i'm looking forward to being able to update this review to 5 stars.
summary: promising, but too much reliance on the limited pure app

reviewText:
this is just a first impressions review.  i kind of felt inclined to do this since the company seems to be very good with customer service and they ask of all their customers to please give feedback.  i won't know for certain how great this flashlight is until i have used it in the field, but my first impression is quite good.  the flashlight comes with spare o rings, and a spare button, which i think is amazing.  it also comes with a special extension adapter so if you want to use a more substantial lithium ion battery you can.  vizeri recommends this, but i have a bunch of nimh batteries and i would like to keep using them so i am going to stick to using them.

my initial impression when holding the flashlight is that it is very well made.  it has a good weight to it without being too heavy.  it fits comfortably in my hand but isn't too fat for my pocket.  i am really pleased with the responsiveness of the on/off button.  it feels heavy duty, and makes a strong click noise when it is pressed.  in the past, i have bought a couple of nebo redline flashlights from trane supply houses.  on both of them, the power switch and intensity selectors always died way before the led was even close to death.  that brings me to the way of selecting the different light intensities.  i am happy with how the selection system works.  you can pretty rapidly switch from one brightness to another.  i am partial to 50% as i almost never have any use for full brightness.  it becomes a hassle when these selectors have you goign through some tedious process to cycle through the different intensities.

i think this flashlight is going to suit me well. i do hvac work and mainly use my flashlight when im crawling through an air handler in some god forsaken drop ceiling.  i so far have absolutely nothing negative to say about this flashlight.  my only wish, was that the end of the flashlight had a magnet on it so i could stick the flashlight to things.  my nebo redline had this feature, and while i wasn't always in the position to use it, when i could stick the flashlight to something i was always super happy that i had it.  i hope that in future editions of this flashlight, that a magnetic base is added.

update: really liked using this flashlight for the most part.  i wish the selector was a bit different though.  i find that i always end up having the thing go to a different intensity selection than what i want.  i wish it had a different selector.  that being said, i had to drop the stars down to 4.  it is still a good flashlight.  i can't seem to find one that is better.  it isn't perfect though.  also, i lost it so i guess i will have to buy a new one.

update 2: well, after using this flashlight for less than a year, it has broken on me. i say less than a year because i actually bought 2 of them on account that i thought i had lost the first one but then found it. the problem  started with the nimh batteries.  i noticed that the thing just didn't seem to last long.  the lights would dim on it rather quickly. the manufacture recommended that you use 18650 batteries so i bought them.  they seemed to work ok for a while.  then one day, this brass ring fell out of one of my flashlights.  i don't know what it was for because the flashlight worked normally for a time. then one day though, it just started flickering.  i tried different batteries but it didn't matter. if i shook the flashight sometimes it would work and sometimes it wouldn't.  i had a second flashlight so i just started using that one.  after a month or two, the same thing happened to that one as well.  it actually started flickering first, then the brass ring fell out of that one. i will not be buying another one of these.  the sad thing is that the best small flashlight i ever had was this one little led mag light flashlight. it fit in the palm of your hand, and it didn't have all these unnecessary modes that i don't have any use for.  it had 100% and 50% brightness.  that's all you need. and it lasted for several years.
summary: pretty good, not perfect.  great customer service though

** update 7/11/16 **
ended up returning this to where i bought it.
started having severe sound issues.
loss if input. sound drop outs. when connected thru hdmi-arc, upon power on the tv and the sound bar both came on just fine.
but the sound bar had lost its input and could not detection active input, even though my dish satellite receiver was on.
had to re-scan the inputs on the bar until it re-established input connection.
tried different hdmi cables hdcp 2.2 hdmi 2.0 compatible. still no improvement. the same issues.
another issue, sound dropouts.
watching south park on the tv, the audio would drop out, then come back in, then drop back out.
i paused the dvr and that caused a loud pop every time i paused the dvr.
the pop was loud and the dogs all went running for the hills.
simply too many issues, sadly, and i returned this vizio sound bar while i still could.
again, too bad. i really wanted this to work.
i was using with an lg tv. maybe using with an actual vizio tv would give better results? maybe not?

(original review)
did not buy from amazon, however would have preferred to. the vizio 2016 sound bar does sound great but had to call vizio tech support to get this working with my new 2016 lg 4k uhd tv. this sound bar uses vizio smartcast, but smartcast is only necessary to connect the sound bar to your home wifi, and for doing firmware updates.
on my lg tv, i set everything correctly using hdmi-arc on the tv and on the sound bar so the lg tv could control the sound bar.
that worked very well. however, i had no sound from the sound bar. the sound bar "sound test" worked ok so i knew the bar was communicating with the rear speakers, and the tv controlled the sound level lights on the bar & the power on-off on the bar, but still no actual sound.
i followed the vizio instructions by pressing the input on the bar, which should have detected audio from the tv and correctly set the input, but still no sound.
called vizio tech support, which is located in america, and they answered within a few minutes, and i explained everything appeared ok except no actual sound. vizio tech had me press that sound bar input and hold the button down until the lights on the sound bar sequenced in pairs up and down on the front of the sound bar. that worked. after pressing and holding down the sound bar input until the lights sequenced in pairs, the tv sound suddenly came in and everything worked great. vizio tech support was excellent. fixed the problem right away first try. sound from the bar is strong and clear. sounds great, even when using a non-vizio tv. but using hdmi-arc to control the bar is the best way to go, if your tv supports hdmi-arc. can't wait to watch those 4k uhd movies from my vudu account.
summary: setup did not go smoothly. great vizio tech support.

i started using the waterfi ipod system in 2013, swimming 3 days a week, 60-90 minutes per workout.  i swim all strokes (including turns) with the ipod, but i have never used it while diving into the pool.

prior to the purchasing the swimactive headphones i used the following:
- the original waterfi short cord headphones that came with the ipod swim kit.
- swimbud waterproof headphones
- water sport waterproof in-ear headphones.

here is a quick overview of my experience with the swimactive competition:
- the original waterfi short cord headphones lasted about a year and frequently got stuck in my ear canal.  cost of these are $30.
- the swimbuds also lasted about a year, but had better resiliency to coming off, and were less prone to leaking.  i preferred these over the waterfi originals.  cost of these are $40.
- the water sport lasted about 5 months.  these were a long cord so they are pretty inconvenient.  the primary advantage is that they are cheap $4.50.

i see many people comment on sound quality.  i find that somewhat amusing as audio fidelity is really the last of my concerns.  my larger concerns are durability and usability.  usability is pretty much the most important part.  what i mean by this is, how often do i have to stop my workout and re-adjust the headphones because i stopped hearing any sound, they hurt my ear, etc. durability is important because of the cost.

initial thoughts for the swimactive's (used since august 10th):
- biggest issue is they do not work well with a cap (which i always swim with).  they sound great until you put the cap on then sound is muffled or totally gets cut off.  then, you need to mess with the cap and headphones to try and get some sound out.  after playing with them i usually get reasonable sound quality out of one side with the other side being very muffled.  note, i did not have this problem with either of the 3 types of headphones i previously purchased.
- comfort, is good.  the design of the headphone is such that they don't hurt while wearing a cap and you don't feel like someone has stuck a finger in your ear for the entire swim.  i also don't believe these will ever come off in your ear canal, which is good.
- cost.  cost is very high at $50.  however, waterfi does have a year warranty, so if they last a year that amounts to ~$1.50 per swim which isn't bad.

again, the jury is out since i've only had them for 2 weeks at this writing.  i'll update this review as i continue to swim (and perhaps get advice on the cap issue).  if the cap issue is solved i'll raise this to 4 starts.  if they last for 2 years, i'll raise it to 5 starts.
-dn
summary: but had better resiliency to coming off

reviewText:
i really wanted to give this product 5 stars because the customer support is really great.  however, i cannot...  i'll keep this as brief as i can, after spending some time with the product and doing a little bit of market research...

a little background on me, i'm not a young man, and i do have a family.  i ride a decent mountain bike, but would love to get into road bikes one day (when there's time, but i digress).  if i'm not doing a pseudo walk/run for 3 miles every other night with my dog, i'm riding it for 6-10 miles.  here in my part of the world, if you don't want to get home dehydrated from the sun, and/or burnt to a crisp, you get your cardio workouts in during the early morning or evening.  evening's are best for me, and that's why i opted to get a couple of lights for the bike.

pros:

-the flash/headlight does have a blinking option which is great for night-riding.  high visibility to on-comers with a blinking light.
-the rear, red led light is brilliant and can flash as well.  again, great for visibility for those creeping from behind.
- installation took a minute or two and required no tools.
- the flash/headlight fits pretty snug into it's harness and removes easily.
- you can tighten-up the light's beam, or spread it out by simply sliding the lens housing forward and backwards up the shaft.
- i do not believe that anyone would find trouble mounting this to "something" on their bike.

cons:

- it's not that bright.  i thought it would be much brighter.  i own cheap flashlights that are "much" brighter.  i guess i was expecting something that would actually help with visibility for me, rather than something that will only serve the purpose of oncoming traffic seeing me.
- the light is only 240 lumens at is highest setting.  i understand that "lumens" can be a misunderstood nomenclature in the lighting industry (i had to do a lot of research on this, myself), but even i have to admit that the "zoom up to 1000x" statement in the product description is a tad misleading to the general public.

on the whole, yes... the product is as described, but it would be best if the consumer does a bit more research on what suits their needs... which segues me into my final con...

- this exact bicycle head/flashlight is being offered on "flea-bay" for less than $6 shipped from our favorite, patent-infringing country in the world.  just look it up as "240 lumen q5 cycling bike bicycle led front head light torch larm with mount" on there and you'll see.  that's how i pulled what little specs are truly out there for this light.

it really pains me to write this review.  i really enjoyed the customer service i received from ti, hence why i'm not sending it back for a refund.  but, i'm just trying to provide a little more feedback on this product than what's listed here on amazon.

so, in short, a+ on my csr experience but i'm not sure the markup justified it.  that blinking red light is only worth about $4-5 here on amazon; so it begs one to ask the question, "where is the other $25 going?"  if my calculations are correct (which they are pretty darn close), if you consider the price of both items... say, $10; that's about a 72% gross margin, and just about a 257% markup on this product (all inclusive).  yikes!  kudos to the owner of this business for supplying a cool little niche in this market.  s/he must have read 4-hour work week by timothy ferriss. :)

again... tough one to review, right?

reviewText:
sound: 5+ stars
these speakers sound incredible especially for their size. i was worried such small speakers wouldn't have full sound but they pack a punch. the sound is quite clear. they fill my deck and reach the back of my yard.

mount: 2 stars
at first i tried mounting these horizontally so they would project under my house's eaves. the first speaker would not stay in place. it kept tilting. i tightened them to the point where the nut broke. i exchanged them for a new pair. i tried a few things with the new pair and finally decided to compromise and mount them vertically. while i feel that they are secure enough not to fall, there is still a little "play" in the mount. it's a ball-and-socket mount. i can get the ball tight in the socket, but the screw protruding from the ball has a little wobble. i was afraid to play with it too much or i'd break another mount.

build quality can't be faulted. so that's comforting...
more later...

reviewText:
i am very dissatified with my logitech mx3100 purchase.  i have owned 4 other logitech keyboard/mouse combinations with the logitech mx duo being my last one.  each of the 4 times i upgraded prior to the mx3100, i was very satisfied with the changes and imporvements that logitech made.  however, the mx3100 is the first to really disappoint me.  here are my problems with the mx3100:

1. the mouse is simply too heavy.  another reviewer mentioned that it just takes getting used to, but i have been using it for over a month, and i still haven't gotten used to it yet (i use it quite often - 6+ hours every day).

2. the function keys are not raised high enough and are too stiff to press.  i prefer using keyboard shortcuts whenever possible, and the mx3100 hinders my ability to quickly use keyboard shortcuts.

3. the volume dial on the keyboard is too small and is difficult to operate because of the lack of decent grooves.

4. the media controls are also not raised high enough and so are difficult to operate.

5. the fast scroll feature is also difficult to operate and get stuck often.

6. the design of the mx duo looked better in my opinion.

i will be moving back to my mx duo very soon.  i regret spending all the money for the mx3100.  i wouldn't suggest the mx3100 to anyone and i would strongly suggest anyone considering purchasing the mx3100 to go to a local store and try it for yourself to see how bad it is.

reviewText:
it's great. i like this keyboard. i have a similar (but smaller) logitech one and i stopped using it in favor of this one. this keyboard has a "no compromise" design. by that i mean that all the other keyboards that have an embedded touch pad cheat a bit in the keyboard buttons layout (e.g. arrows, home, delete etc.) to save some space. this one has a standard layout with a numeric pad plus a touch pad. the side effect is that it's a little bit longer then a regular keyboard, but not by much. so i can use it in bed for fun or for more serious tasks (e.g. i code computer programs on my bed using this keyboard).

i gave it 4 starts (and not 5) because, while i appreciate the conservative design, it would have been nice to have some multimedia media buttons (e.g. volume, play/pause etc.) without having to press the fn button. don't get me wrong, it does have multimedia buttons, but you have to press a combo of the fn button + one of the f7, f8 etc keys to use them. which may prove less then "ideal", if say you're watching a movie at night with the lights off.

lastly, i realized it consumes battery a little fast then other keyboards of its class (e.g. with touch pads)... i can't really penalize it for that because, again, it has a "no compromise" design (standard layout + touch pad + numeric pad), and it has a very conveniently place on/off switch behind it. so i just started turning it off when i am not using it and got pretty good battery life (over 3 months i think of the top of my head... didn't really measure.)

this  camera has multiple problems , mostly on the usability side.
the video image is great but the camera is just not practical to use for home surveillance.
1. the camera is getting multiple complaints online for their plugins which are required for it to work on browsers such as chrome or firefox. i could not get it to work with chrome and their tech support admitted they were having problems and suggested i used firefox. well, that didn't work either. they only way i could get to work was with a chrome plugin that opens their own browser app and then you can see live video and operate the camera. so you login in and get a screen that says "please click here to download and install the plugin" then you click that and get another browser tab with their plugin on it and you have to click "launch app". that opens their proprietary browser in a separate window. then you have to type in your camera's web address in their proprietary browser. then after waiting a few more seconds you finally see the camera video.
2. the problem with this browser app is that it is not resizable so if you want to watch your home from work you have this giant camera live view browser that can not be minimized and run in the corner of your screen.  i do not have this problem with foscam software. foscam works perfectly in browsers.
3. ftp upload does not seem to work right. when testing the upload it will say it could not connect, other times it says it connects and uploaded successfully but i look on the hosting site and it shows a folder in the directory i specified and a weird file that is not an image file. i don't even know that is. this works perfectly on foscam for motion detection image stores.
3. the user interface is extremely cumbersome and complicated. i am a software developer and even i had trouble with it. even setting the motion detection area is hard using the mouse. you drag but the mouse position does not reflect the area you are settings.  there is a "threshold" feature in motion detection but i don't even know what  that setting does. impossible to figure out. and they don't call it motion detection
4. when you click on help it brings up a dialog that i can't even understand with links that when you click on them they do nothing.
5. the tech support people have a thick indian accent and you can't understand what they are saying. and from my last conversation, they couldn't understand me. i kept saying browser on computer and they kept saying "what kind of phone". i was on on the phone with one guy for 30 minutes and spent most of my time saying " what?" they don't even know their own software.

reviewText: first impressions are very good with this radio. it installed it very quickly. i have a honda civic hybrid so i was able to use the factory bracket to secure it in place. it doesnt use a standard wire pin out on the plug. it fit okay but not perfect. i couldn't find the perfect hole configuration to adjust the screen more towards the driver. wiring was pretty straight forward i only hooked up the gps antenna and usb extentions. im not hooking up a back up camera just yet. so far ive downloaded youtube and used the usb mirror software. all worked great. the audio quality on thw factory speakers was impressive considering i wasn't expecting much. signal comes in strong but i don't use radio much. the mirror software on my phone worked good. it was a bit complicated to set up initially but once i did it worked great other than a little lag. but the same can be said with almost any mirror software. my 2017 impalla has the same issue but more lag.  i like how the chassis is slim, it allows more instalation options. after warm up it takes very little time to turn on. so far the value out weights and issue i have ran across thus far. i bought it on lightning deal but if i would have known how well it worked i would have paid full price. im going to buy some other brands to try them out for my other vehicles just to see how they  differ. the things i would change so far: added sd card storage, ability to update os, the ability to turn the radio off easier, maybe i haven't figured it out yet. the ui is a bit clunky. but well worth the price so far.

reviewText:
do not buy if you are going to install windows 7.  client purchased 5 of these and 2 hps.  hps wonderful setup and working.  asus has no customer service nor support.  client must have windows 7 pro to interface with medical i.h.s. what a pain to setup windows 7 on these boxes.  so far one dead bios - 1.5 pcs with windows 7 installed.  this is almost a week of time lost and the need to return not only the pc boxes but the ssd and the ram.
you can install windows 7 but plan on spending more time setting up than you will like.  i cannot recommend this product to anyone.  asus customer service basically told me that they are not interested in us buying the remain 25 units that we need to schedule for replacement this year.  go with hp is what there person told me.  wow!!!  that is incredible!!!
plan on spending time researching the usb 3 issues and potential fixes.  plan on windows not accepting any of the drivers on the asus support disc while trying to install.  expect many glitches and failures as part of the search for incredible experience.  once you remove the screws, only put the bare minimum back until you are fully finished.
our approach is to get the os installed enough to pull the ssd from the asus and plug it into an adapter and copy and paste drive files to the ssd from the download.  make sure to unzip them first. some may not work and you will have them nag you each time on start up until you hunt them down and kill them.
asus warns not to change the bios but you will have to make changes if you plan on using windows 7.

once you can get usb drivers and network adapter up, you can install the most current driver updates.  if you opt to install from the cd/dvd you need to be aware that the bloat ware will be there.  time to un-install and then the hours of window updates.
we have built many workstations, servers, gaming pcs and high end computers but these little boxes caused us and our client too much grief to be of any value.
save time and go with anything other than asus if you think you might need their help. negative stars for "incredible" bad support from asus.
when you claim that win 7 can be used on these little guys - you get the one star.
when the internal battery goes, the pc is a disposable as you cannot access the board.  well hopefully it is out of warranty and you can tear into it but not while under warranty. another one star rating.
nice looking box.  3 star.
summary: so much big pain from such a small pc.  may be ok with win 10 but win 7 should be avoided on this. no support asus...

after my sennheiser cx300 broke after 2 years of use, i thought of upgrading to these higher quality headphones. i used the er6i for 3 months and the cables just tore snapped. it was like...????!!!! i had used a cheaper headphones for 2 years and this er6i only survived for 3 months?

reviewText:
we have an unlisted phone number that is only given out to maybe 20 members of our family.  this device can be set up to only allow our house phones to ring if the call is from one of these 20 "white listed" numbers entered into its memory.  otherwise, it will block the house phones from ringing and our internet phone answering service will answer after 5 rings.  we set the answering service message up with no identification of who we are and a request for the caller to leave their name / company name and telephone number and the first and last name of the person they are attempting to contact.  this arrangement stops telemarketing cold-calls and all the other nonsense completely, at the same time it offers any legitimate callers the opportunity to leave a message.  we can then add them onto the "white list" in this ring blocking device if we wish.

warning, programing the device is a bit awkward.  we suggest you carefully read the instructions as well as other operation hints on the company web site.  also, this device has been reported to block caller id information from appearing on the house phones plugged in after the device.  in our case (panasonic kx-tga939t wireless handsets), caller id information does appear on the house phone if the number is "white listed" on the device and allowed to ring through.

this unit has now worked flawlessly for about two months and was worth the cost and time to install.  silence!

update:  this and a second unit are still working flawlessly after three years.  keep the programming instructions where you can find them in case you need to change settings - not very user friendly.  but, performance has been perfect.  our 25-year unlisted personal phone number has been targeted now for over four years by a series of unethical bill collectors who believe some person unknown to us lives here.  nothing, including cease and desist orders from the state attorney's office stopped these sobs.  they just sell the account to a new collection agency.  the "white list" strategy outlined above has worked perfectly.  no matter how many times they change their caller id number; no matter what company buys the collection account; no matter what spoofing ploy they adopt, our days and night proceed uninterrupted.  our only bother is laughing at their latest ploy ("you have repaired diamond jewelery that you need to pick up" is one of the funniest), and erasing all the messages every week or so.
summary: excellent tech solution with a few notes

easy to use, and user friendly. i also have to admit i got mine on ebay, as i have all the accessories. way less expensive than amazon.
check it out.

reviewText:
i'm a 100 word-per-minute touch typist and this is the only mini keyboard i've found that lets me come close to that.  i loved the full sized verion of this keyboard for the regular ipad, so when logitech introduced a mini version, i was excited.

 it's close to perfect except:

-the tab key unfortunately requires the simultanous use of the function key, and unfortunately they were placed on the same side of the keyboard so there is no easy way to tab while touch typing, as it requires two fingers from the same hand in a combination that i've never needed to use before.  not a deal breaker, but a pretty big bummer.  i get that they had to make sacrifices due to such small real estate, but that one seems like a poor choice.

-the semi-colon/colon key and quote/apostrophe key are both half-sized, which places the return key right where the apostrophe would normally be.  this means i often hit return and skip down a line when i didn't mean to.  fortunately, after a few minutes of typing with this keyboard, my fingers mostly remember and adjust for this, so it's not quite as irritating as the pror issue to me (though finding yourself typing on an unintended line can be unfortunate.)

-the magnet that holds the cover closed and turns off the ipad mini isn't strong enough to keep it tightly closed or turned off, so i often notice the light beaming away inside my purse.  not so great for ipad battery life.  i deal with this by keeping my original apple ipad mini flip cover on the front and then just putting the keybard on over that, making a sandwhich with the apple cover in the middle.  the hinge magnets hold just fine like this.  this is fine with me as i don't always want to use the keyboard and i do still want a cover.

aside from those two keyboard issues, both sacrificed made to maintain a near-normal keyboard layout in a tiny space, this keyboard is nice to type on.  the keys feel smooth, and although they are small, my fingers find them easily (i have small hands, though.)  it's pretty close to the perfect keyboard and definitely still a good purchase, despite the issues.
summary: almost perfect; best mini keyboard on the market

i bought these ear buds to replace the iconic factory ipod ones. i find after use that i am happy and slightly impressed, but i'm left feeling as if i should have just stayed with the originals. i thought the sound was great and superior to the factory buds, and it also cancels out some noise because of the insulation surrounding the earpieces.

the one thing that really stands out to me about these that almost, and still may be a deal breaker for me, negatively i might add, is the separation element in the middle of the cord of these ear buds. they have a plug in in the middle of these cords, for universal ability i guess, that gets caught in everything that seems to come near or in contact with me. it also weighs down on my ears, where i find it a problem that these ear buds keep popping out. this extension tool feels exactly like a weight barring down on my ears, trying to pull them out where i find myself constantly having to rearrange and readjust the ear pieces themselves. additionally, the cover of the speakers feels like cardboard, and as such is prone to obstruction and destruction so be careful there.

to sum up, i think they are worth the money you pay for them, but have severe annoyances along with poor construction. i would say they are just a smidgen above factory buds, and you could probably find better ones out there for that matter.

reviewText:
i have to be honest - i really wasn't expecting much for a cheap (sub-40 dollar) microsoft branded mouse.  so i was honestly a bit pleasantly surprised when using the sculpt comfort mouse.

first, the potential negatives:
battery life - it uses two aa batteries and has an on/off switch (which i will probably not remember to use half the time).  i haven't run out the batteries yet, but i haven't used it extensively.  i'll need to see how long the batteries actually last with practical use, because that will definitely influence the review.
weight & size - the mouse is a bit hefty.  personally i like this (i don't like very light mice, they feel too delicate) but i can see how it would be burdensome for travelling.  its not slim enough to easily slip in some bag pocket either.

now the positives:
feel - its actually very comfortable, at least for me.  i have larger hands, so smaller mice are hard for me to use without contorting my fingers.  this one i didn't notice that so mauch.
weight & size - as stated before, i like these aspects, but i can see how they would be negatives.
responsiveness - the mouse connects quickly and easily via bluetooth, and is very responsive.  i noticed no lag or delay.
tracking - i was pleasantly surprised by this.  the mouse tracked well on a variety of surfaces, and seemed very accurate in its tracking.  i couldn't find any dpi information though, and i doubt it compares to a really high end gaming mouse (i have one but its in poor condition, and not a good comparison).
the blue 'touch' button - this is the fun addition to the mouse, and i actually like it.  i'm using windows 7, so the functionality is limited.  for me.  the big thing i like is that the 'back' feature doesn't actually go back in a webpage or some such, but instead pops up the tile viewer to easily sort through your open programs.  other reviewers have complained about the vibration, but i like that tangible feeling it gives.  its personal preference.

now, is this thing really twice as good as a cheap twenty dollar mouse?  that i'm not sure of.  i think the tracking and responsiveness is more solid, and it feels more solidly built, but i don't know that its actually twice as good.  that said, i do think its a good value for the money, in terms of the quality you get.  definitely a very solid mid-cost mouse.

after the hype of the keynote in san francisco in january, i decided to finally take the plunge and revisit the world of apple after an absentia of >20 years. yes, my last apple was a 48kb iie.

so here is my mini-review after 1 week of use.

packaging and aesthetics : excellent, light weight, fantastic build quality.

lcd display: nice, but not as nice as the fujitsu/sony's

os: very nice os compared to windows xp. easy to use. but one big caveat. i am surprised that os x took up so much space! found a 2gb folder with nothing but printer drivers. iworks is 2gb nb ms office is only 561 mb. on a fresh mbp, almost 20 gb of harddisk spaced used at the outset....so for all those who think windows is bloatware think again. os x might be worse in this respect.

battery life: average 3hrs of use. 2hrs + if playing a dvd.

features:

pros: isight built in. magsafe to prevent my 4 year old from tripping. remote control!

cons:where is the fw 800, dual layer burner and my modem!

performance: fast with optimized universal binary software.

packaged software:

pros:ilife 06- great!,front row- fantastic, dashboard!

cons: should have bundled iworks for free rather than just a trial.

software availablity: most stuff that you do on a pc is available. one big hole is in the games dept though.

overall, my conversion to the macworld has been an easy one although i have to admit i won't be throwing away my pc as the workplace remains pc only.

conclusion: a solid 4.5 stars
summary: macbook pro... thoughts from a life long pc user.

this is a great product *if* you're technically inclined enough not to mind hacking around with some linux tools. using the "unslung" firmware, this little device becomes a versatile server for your web site, your music, or even a multimedia recorder.

it's quiet and doesn't consume much power. i use it as a music server for streaming my mp3s elsewhere in the house over the wireless network. in the past, my big noisy spare pc would be devoted to that task. now my office can be quiet while the "slug" does the dirty work.

if you want plug and play network attached storage, this will do that as well. you'll hear some complaining that it only mounts unix filesystems. that's not really a big deal if you can boot into linux occasionally (knoppix or ubuntu have "live cds" that can boot you without changing your system). if you really need everything to have a graphical user interface or a windows logo, steer clear, but don't ruin the fun for the rest of us. :-)
summary: does what it should -- and a whole lot more.

reviewText:
ok. your computer motherboard has an unused 2x5 male-pinned header that serves up two usb ports. [those are usually there in case you happen to have internal devices that expect to be powered, controlled and/or configured as usb devices.]

and your normal-height computer case has an unused slot in the back.

who can't use more external usb ports, right? so plop down the $8 + s/h get this thing.

the wires are short. i measured them at exactly 7.5" from base of the usb port to the very end of the wire header. since the usb ports actually sit an inch or more above the mobo, in practical terms, you're not going to get much more than 5 inches of reach. if you need an 12" extension cable, look at item cab-167 vended at frozencpu. even the wire color is a match.

there was a catch. the female end of this gizmo that plugs into the motherboard was mis-pinned. swap the pins into the correct location and you're good-2-go.

on the motherboard, the correct pinout for a single usb internal header is:

  pin1, red, +5v (power)
  pin2, white, usb- (data)
  pin3, green, usb+ (data)
  pin4, black, ground
  pin5, void (or an optional, heavier-gauge black wire for sgnd, signal ground)

i rec'd this gizmo pinned as

  pin1-red
  pin2-void
  pin3-white
  pin4-green
  pin5-black

i had to carefully move the female pins around to correct this.

use the smallest jeweler's (or eyeglass repair) flat-tip screwdriver you can find. gently and ever-so-slightly lift the small restraining flap in the plastic terminator--the end to lift is found at the lower edge of the little open square that reveals a part of the pin. the pin should slide/drop right out. then slide the pin into the correct slot. the pin will click in place behind the restraining flap. don't bust the flap off or ... well, you know.

while this fix is simple enough, you can be sure that thousands of customers created immense amounts of costs and work for the manufacturer and vendors when they simply returned these things after finding the usb ports didn't work.

as such, you can also be sure that somewhere, in some distant part of the world, the worker who built tens of thousands of these incorrectly -- a worker whose only job description was "insert pin1 as red, pin2 as white, ..." -- has now returned to a career in agriculture.

update: i bought another one of these in august, 2011. it came (correctly) pinned as:

pin1-red
pin2-white
pin3-green
pin4-black
pin5-black

i guess the first one was just a one-in-a-zillion dud.
summary: works fine .. but you'll spend a few minutes re-pinning it.

reviewText:
pros: price
cons: slow, muddy bass, 60hz hum at high volume setting with no muted audio

with over 700 mostly five star reviews and huge discount for discontinued product, i was sure i can't go wrong with psw505. but i was. if you never had any sub before, this probably will meet your expectations as for less than $200 you get massive heavy well built cube able to shake your room well. but is it all what defines decent sub sound quality? certainly not.

first of all, this sub must have really poor amplifier/supply design as it produces audible hum with no signal being inputted. this 60hz noise level follow the volume setting and is also affected by the length of connecting lf input rca cable. which tells me about poor design of the input circuit as well as power supply filtration including proper ground noise decoupling. this is not 70's or 80's anymore and any active subwoofer should be absolutely silent when no lf signal is fed. period.

secondly, quick look at used woofer design might give a clue of why produces bass is slow and muddy comparing to similarly priced competitive products. although driver is listed as 12 inch, the actual diaphragm diameter is little over 8 inches suspended on enormously wide surround suspension which for sure allow woofer to work with large displacement but it produces lots of distortion and may slow the bass reproduction which in case of psw505 is clearly heard.

lastly, this is back vented subwoofer design. this means most of people may have hard time to position the sub in order to get deep unidirectional distributed bass. the vent port blows as the main drives blow directional so the bass intensity dramatically changes as you change listener position against it or rotate subwoofer on its axis sitting in fixed position. there are plenty budget subs around with bottom vent design and these are able to produce unidirectional bass which makes sub location flexible and allows entire floor to distribute lows, which makes a big difference in sound scene not only for watching action packed movies but when listening traditional stereo in 2.1 mode.

with that said, i cannot recommend psw505. my experience with this product seems to explain such heavily discount offered for already discontinued product which apparently performed below acceptable performance level which i define as minimum required for decent ht systems out there.
summary: product heavily discounted for good reason may disappoint quality bass seeking users

this is kodak's entry into the 3 megapixel market (and some reports indicate that this is the first of kodak's digital cameras to be designed  by kodak japan), and considering that kodak did so well at 2mp with the  dc280, one expects a formidable digital camera, and gets it, for the most  part.  this is my second kodak digital camera and i've continued to  purchase kodak because with digital cameras the camera is also the film and  no one knows how to make film quite like kodak, a la kodachrome.  the  previous dc280 is a point and shoot camera only, and while the dc4800  offers manual control of many functions, it still basicaslly a point and  shoot camera - for instance, with the dc4800 no control of focus is  possible, and if you want to change shutter speed you have to go through  several levels of menu (no less than 10 button presses to get to the  shutter speed menu and then as much as another 12 to choose the speed).  hopefully, as the digital era progresses digital cameras will become more  like the slrs of old with manual control of every function and all the  controls on the body of the camera, rather then buried deep in menus.  (i  understand olympus is about to release its e10 which is like a digital slr;  however the price will be about $2000.)

the positives -

this is hands down the best protective case for my ipod that i've ever owned.  it is just a little bulky, but it's still a whole lot smaller than the cd case i used to keep in my car.  not only does the rubber case protect the ipod from just about every conceivable type of damage but immersion in water, the thick plastic screen cover protects the screen from all types of damage, as well.  the sticky rubber cover also keeps your ipod from sliding all over your car while underway.  this case has done a fantastic job of keeping my ipods looking like new.
i have used this case with 30 gb and 160 gb ipods and it fits both like a glove.  a rubber filler is included to occupy the extra space when used with the 30 gb ipod so it still fits snugly.
the one issue that other reviewers seem to have with this case is the fact that its bulk doesn't allow the case to be used with an ipod dock.  to overcome this spend 6-10 bucks on an ipod dock extension cable and your problems are solved.  they're all over amazon.  the extension cable plugs into your dock, then into your ipod, so the ipod doesn't have to fit directly into the dock anymore.  problem solved!
i would absolutely recommend this tough little case to anyone that uses an ipod on the go and doesn't want to have to worry about damaging it.
